title: Testing materials: how sure can a test make us?

summary.text: Drop a rubber ball ten times from the same height, and it bounces to ten slightly different heights. So when a marble bounces lower than the ball, is the marble really worse, or is that just the ordinary wobble in every test? Your child drops balls again and again, draws every bounce as a dot, and finds out when a difference is real. Along the way they meet three ways a test can fool us: the material varies, our measuring is rough, and we hope for an answer. Scientists have a trick against each one.
summary.art: A kitchen floor with a ruler taped to a wall, a rubber ball at the top of its bounce, and a sheet of paper on the floor covered in rows of dots, one row for each ball.

intro.hook: You drop a rubber ball from the height of your hip, and it bounces to 31 centimetres. You drop a table-tennis ball from the same height, and it bounces to 33 centimetres. So the table-tennis ball is bouncier. Is that right? Now drop the rubber ball again. This time it bounces to 34.
intro.text: The same ball gave two different numbers, with nothing changed. So can one drop tell you anything at all? This is the next question in testing materials. In the Class 3 unit you learned to change one thing at a time and to repeat a test three times. Here you go a step further. You will repeat a test ten times, draw every result as a dot, and ask how big the ordinary wobble is. Only a difference bigger than the wobble can be believed. You will also learn why your own eyes and hopes can fool you, and how scientists test in the dark on purpose.
intro.art: A child kneeling by a bouncing rubber ball, with two different numbers floating in the air above two drops from the same hand.

outcomes: I can repeat a test many times and show all the results as dots on a dot plot, so I can see how much they vary.
I can find the range and the middle value of a set of results, and say what each one tells me.
I can tell when a difference between two materials is real, and when it is smaller than the ordinary wobble.
I can explain the difference between a rough measuring tool, a wrong measuring tool, and a tool that is fine but used badly.
I can explain how my own hopes can change a result, and run a blind test with secret codes and random order.
I can plan a wear test that copies real use, and say what the test leaves out.
I can write a claim, evidence and reasoning that also says how sure I am, and why.

terms.meaning: The small differences you get when you do the same thing again and again. Even a careful test gives different numbers each time.
terms.example: Ten drops of the same rubber ball gave ten slightly different bounce heights.
terms.art: Ten rubber ball drops drawn as ten bounce marks of slightly different heights on a wall ruler.

terms.meaning: How far apart your results are, from the smallest to the biggest. A wide spread means the results wobble a lot.
terms.example: The bounce heights of one ball spread from 30 to 35 centimetres.
terms.art: A row of dots along a ruler, some close together and some far apart, with an arrow across the whole row.

terms.meaning: The smallest result and the biggest result, and the gap between them. You say it as 'from 30 to 35', or you say the gap, which is 5.
terms.example: The marble bounced from 23 to 28 centimetres. Its range is 5 centimetres.
terms.art: A number line with a bracket from the smallest dot to the biggest dot.

terms.meaning: A picture with a number line and one dot for every result. Dots that are the same stack up. You can see the spread at one glance.
terms.example: A dot plot of ten bounce heights, with a tall stack of dots at 32 centimetres.
terms.art: A number line with stacks of dots above it, like a small bar chart made of dots.

terms.meaning: Put your results in order. The one in the middle is the middle value. If there are two in the middle, find the number halfway between them. Scientists call it the median.
terms.example: The ten bounces in order were 30, 30, 31, 31, 32, 32, 33, 33, 34, 35. The two middle ones are 32 and 32, so the middle value is 32.
terms.art: Ten number cards in a row, with the two middle cards glowing.

terms.meaning: Add all the results, then divide by how many there are. It is the number each result would be if they were all shared out equally.
terms.example: The ten bounce heights add up to 321. Divided by 10, the average is 32.1 centimetres.
terms.art: Ten stacks of coins levelled out into ten equal stacks.

terms.meaning: The few things you test, taken from a much bigger bunch of the same thing. A sample is only useful if it is a fair picture of the bunch.
terms.example: You test ten strips from one roll of kitchen paper. The ten strips are the sample. The whole roll is the bunch.
terms.art: A handful of rice grains taken from a big sack.

terms.meaning: A difference between two materials that is bigger than the ordinary wobble in each one. You can believe it.
terms.example: The marble's bounces were all lower than every bounce of the rubber ball. That is a real difference.
terms.art: Two dot plots side by side with a clear gap between them.

terms.meaning: When the results for two materials share some of the same numbers. If they overlap a lot, you cannot tell the materials apart with that test.
terms.example: The rubber ball bounced from 30 to 35 centimetres and the table-tennis ball from 31 to 36. The two ranges overlap.
terms.art: Two dot plots drawn on one number line with the middle part covered by both.

terms.meaning: The small gap between the number you wrote down and the true size. Every measurement has some. It does not mean you made a mistake.
terms.example: Two people read the same bounce and wrote 31 and 33 centimetres.
terms.art: Two people looking at the same ruler from different angles and reading different marks.

terms.meaning: A fault in a measuring tool that is always the same size. A ruler with a chipped end starts at 1 centimetre instead of 0, so every reading is too big by 1.
terms.example: A worn ruler that starts at 0.5 centimetres adds half a centimetre to everything.
terms.art: A ruler with its first centimetre broken off, and a finger on the broken end.

terms.meaning: The smallest step a tool can show. A ruler marked in millimetres cannot show a tenth of a millimetre.
terms.example: A kitchen scale that moves in steps of 5 grams cannot tell a 2 gram difference.
terms.art: A ruler with tiny marks, and a magnifying glass over two marks.

terms.meaning: Giving nearly the same reading every time you measure the same thing. A precise tool can still be wrong, if it has a zero error.
terms.example: A bathroom scale that says 31.2, 31.3 and 31.2 kilograms for the same bag is precise.
terms.art: Three arrows all stuck close together in the target, but far from the middle.

terms.meaning: Giving a reading close to the true size. An accurate tool gives the right answer on average, even if single readings wobble.
terms.example: Readings of 29, 32 and 31 for a bag that really weighs 31 kilograms are accurate on average.
terms.art: Arrows scattered around the middle of the target.

terms.meaning: A push on the result that always goes the same way. Your hopes can cause it without you noticing.
terms.example: A tester who hopes the red cloth wins pulls a little gentler on it, and does not know she is doing it.
terms.art: A set of scales with a thumb pressing down on one side.

terms.meaning: A test where the tester does not know which sample is which, so hopes cannot change what they do.
terms.example: A friend puts secret codes on three cloths, and you test them without knowing which is which.
terms.art: A child with a scarf over their eyes, feeling three cloths labelled with secret letters.

terms.meaning: Chosen by chance, with no pattern, such as by drawing paper chits from a bowl. A random order does not favour any sample.
terms.example: Draw four chits to decide which cloth is tested first.
terms.art: Four folded paper chits in a bowl, and a hand picking one.

terms.meaning: A sample where you do nothing to the thing you are testing. It shows what happens anyway.
terms.example: A paper strip left dry while the other strips are wetted. If the dry strip also changes, something else is changing it.
terms.art: Two identical strips, one with a drop of water and one left dry, side by side.

terms.meaning: A test that really measures what you care about. Tests that are easy to do are not always valid.
terms.example: Pulling a sari thread until it snaps does not tell you if the sari will last in the wash. Washing it ten times does.
terms.art: A sari beside a washing machine and a thread being pulled, with a question mark between them.

terms.meaning: A test that rubs, bends or washes a material again and again to see how it wears out.
terms.example: Rubbing a cloth on sandpaper and counting rubs until a hole appears is a wear test.
terms.art: A cloth stretched over a katori being slid along a sheet of sandpaper.

terms.meaning: A test that squeezes years of use into a few minutes by using a harsher rub than real life.
terms.example: A machine that bends a jeans knee 10,000 times in an afternoon tests what a year of walking would do.
terms.art: A calendar with a year crossed out, next to a machine bending a jeans knee.

terms.meaning: To check a measuring tool against something you trust, and to fix or note any error.
terms.example: Put the ruler beside a new ruler to see if both give the same reading for the same strip.
terms.art: Two rulers laid edge to edge with their marks lined up.

terms.meaning: Three sentences. The claim says what you think is true. The evidence says what you saw. The reasoning says why the evidence supports the claim.
terms.example: Claim: the ball bounces higher. Evidence: ten dots all above the other ball's dots. Reasoning: the gap is bigger than the wobble.
terms.art: A notebook with three lines, marked by a speech bubble, an eye and a lightbulb.

terms.meaning: How many times stronger than the biggest load we expect we make a thing. It protects us from the weakest piece and from surprises.
terms.example: A lift cable that will only ever carry 1,000 kilograms is made to hold several times that.
terms.art: A cable holding a lift, with a much bigger weight drawn beside it to show how much more it could hold.

explanations.concept: The same test gives a different number every time
explanations.definition: Variation means that repeating a test gives results that are close but not equal. Every test has it.
explanations.description: Drop a rubber ball from 50 centimetres onto the kitchen floor ten times. It will not bounce to the same height ten times. You might see 31, 33, 30, 34 and so on. Nothing went wrong. Many tiny things change from drop to drop. Your fingers let go a little differently. The ball lands on a slightly different spot of the floor. It spins a little. A speck of dust is under it once. The ball's rubber is a tiny bit warmer after a few bounces. Each tiny thing nudges the bounce up or down by a little. Together they make a spread of results. Scientists call this variation. Variation is in every test of every material, including tests done by experts in a laboratory. It is not a fault of the child or the ball. It is how the world is.
examples: Ten drops of one rubber ball gave heights from 30 to 35 centimetres.
Ten strips cut from the same roll of kitchen paper held different numbers of coins before tearing.
Ten grains of the same rice are never exactly the same length.
explanations.art: A rubber ball dropped ten times, with ten different bounce marks on a wall ruler and a few of the tiny causes drawn as little labels: finger, dust, spin, spot on the floor.
explanations.context: Last year you repeated a test three times and took the middle value. This card explains why three was only a start, and why the numbers are never the same.

explanations.concept: Spread, range and the dot plot
explanations.definition: The range of a set of results is the gap between the smallest and the biggest. A dot plot shows every result as a dot on a number line.
explanations.description: To see the spread, draw a dot plot. First draw a number line along the bottom of a page, from your smallest result to your biggest. Then make one dot above the line for every result. If two results are equal, stack one dot on top of the other. Now look. Where the dots pile up tall, results are common. Where the line is empty, results are rare. The range is the gap from the smallest dot to the biggest. For the rubber ball the smallest bounce was 30 and the biggest was 35, so the range is 5 centimetres. A range of 5 tells you how much to trust a single drop. One drop could be out by up to 5. A dot plot shows this at a glance, and a plain list of ten numbers does not.
examples: Smallest 30, biggest 35: the range is 5 centimetres.
A tall stack of dots at 32 and 33 shows that most drops landed there.
An empty space on the number line next to a lone dot is a hint to look at that drop again.
explanations.art: A hand-drawn dot plot of ten bounce heights on squared paper, with a bracket across all the dots labelled range.
explanations.context: After a test you have ten numbers. This card shows how to draw all ten so that you can see the spread with your own eyes.

explanations.concept: Is the difference real? Compare the gap with the wobble
explanations.definition: A difference is real when it is bigger than the ordinary wobble. If the ranges overlap a lot, the test cannot tell the materials apart.
explanations.description: Look at the three made-up balls. The rubber ball's middle value was 32 centimetres. The table-tennis ball's was 34. The marble's was 25. Which differences are worth trusting? Compare each gap with the wobble. The rubber ball and the table-tennis ball differ by 2, but each one wobbles over a range of 5. Their ranges overlap a lot, from 31 to 35. A rubber ball sometimes bounces higher than a table-tennis ball. So this test cannot say which is bouncier. Now compare the rubber ball and the marble. The marble's highest bounce, 28, is lower than the rubber ball's lowest, 30. Their ranges do not overlap at all. That is a real difference. A good rule of thumb: if the gap between the middle values is smaller than the range of each ball, say 'we cannot tell'. If the ranges do not touch, say 'there is a real difference'. Scientists have more careful rules, but this one already stops many mistakes.
examples: Rubber 30 to 35 and table-tennis 31 to 36 overlap, so we cannot tell.
Rubber 30 to 35 and marble 23 to 28 do not touch, so the difference is real.
If you test with 30 drops instead of 10, the ranges may widen a little, but the middle values settle down.
explanations.art: Three dot plots drawn on one number line: the rubber ball and the table-tennis ball overlapping in the middle, and the marble sitting clear to the left.
explanations.context: Two balls gave different middle values. This card explains how to decide whether that difference means anything.

chart.title: Middle value of 10 drops for each ball (made-up)
chart.note: The bars look different, but the ranges tell the real story. The rubber ball and the table-tennis ball overlap. The marble does not.

explanations.definition: Repeating a test makes luck matter less. It cannot fix an error that always pushes the same way.
explanations.description: More tries make the middle value steadier. One drop can be far from the usual. The middle of three is better. The middle of ten is better still. But there is a limit. Ten tries is much better than three. A hundred is only a little better than ten. And no number of tries can fix a ruler with a chipped end, or a tester who always hopes for the same answer. Repeating a test reduces the effect of luck, but it does not remove an error that always pushes the same way. Also, tries must be fair copies of each other. Ten strips cut from ten different rolls, bought at ten different shops, are a better picture of 'kitchen paper' than ten strips next to each other on one roll. That is why scientists think about the sample. The sample must look like the whole bunch. Engineers who test lift cables break many pieces, taken from different places along different reels.
examples: Three drops of one ball: one lucky drop can mislead. Ten drops: much safer.
Ten strips from one roll tell you about that roll. Strips from five rolls tell you about the brand.
A hundred drops of a ball with a taped ruler on the wall that sits 1 centimetre too high will all be wrong by 1 centimetre.
explanations.art: A scale balancing three tries on one side and ten tries on the other, with a thumb pressing the scale down on a side marked 'ruler with a chipped end'.
explanations.context: A test with ten tries is better than one with three. This card explains how many tries are enough and what repeating cannot fix.

explanations.concept: Measuring is rough: error, zero error and resolution
explanations.definition: Error is the small gap between a reading and the true size. Zero error is a fault that is always the same size. Resolution is the smallest step a tool can show.
explanations.description: Every measuring tool has a smallest step it can show. This is its resolution. A school ruler shows millimetres, so a reading of 31.4 centimetres is a guess between two marks. Every reading also has a small error, because eyes, fingers and light are not perfect. Two people reading the same bounce may write 31 and 33. That is measurement error, and it is normal. A second kind of fault is different. If a ruler has a chipped end, every reading is wrong by the same amount. That is a zero error. You can check for it by putting the ruler beside another ruler, which is called calibrating. Scientists describe good measuring with two words. Precise means that readings agree with each other. Accurate means that readings are close to the true size. A target shows the difference. Arrows close together but far from the middle are precise but not accurate. Arrows scattered evenly around the middle are accurate on average, but not precise. The best tools are both.
examples: A phone video of a bounce, played slowly, lets you read the top of the bounce from one frame, so the error is smaller than reading it by eye.
A ruler that begins at 1 centimetre has a zero error of 1 centimetre.
A kitchen scale with steps of 5 grams cannot show a difference of 2 grams.
explanations.art: Two targets drawn side by side: one with arrows tightly grouped near the edge, and one with arrows scattered around the centre, each labelled with its word.
explanations.context: Two people read the same bounce and wrote different numbers. This card explains rough measuring, a chipped ruler and why we check our tools.

explanations.concept: Hopes fool us: bias and the blind test
explanations.definition: Bias is a push on a result that always goes one way. A blind test stops the tester knowing which sample is which.
explanations.description: Imagine you are sure the red cloth is the strongest. You pull the red cloth and the blue cloth to see which tears first. Without knowing it, you may pull the blue one a little faster, because you want to see it lose. This is called bias. It is not cheating. It happens without our noticing, even to expert scientists. A famous case is a horse called Clever Hans. In Berlin, about 1904, people thought he could do sums, because he tapped the right number with his hoof. In 1907 a psychologist named Oskar Pfungst showed that Hans was reading tiny movements of the person who asked the question. The questioners nodded very slightly as the taps reached the right number. They did not know they did it. When the questioner did not know the answer, Hans got it wrong. The fix for bias is a blind test. A helper puts secret codes on the samples and keeps the list. The tester does not know which is which until all the results are written down. Medicine trials work the same way. Often the helper also draws the order of testing from a bowl, which is the random part.
examples: Judges at a talent show who cannot see the singers can judge only the voice.
Researchers testing a new medicine give half the patients a plain pill, and neither the patients nor the doctors know who got which.
A friend puts a secret letter on each of three cloths and keeps the list until you have finished testing.
explanations.art: A horse in a courtyard tapping his hoof while a man in a long coat stands very still, with a small arrow showing a tiny nod of the man's head.
explanations.context: You may think your own eyes would never be unfair. This card shows how hopes sneak into a test, and how scientists test in the dark on purpose.

explanations.concept: A fair order: why we draw lots
explanations.definition: A random order is chosen by chance, so no sample always gets an early slot or a late slot.
explanations.description: Suppose you test four cloths and always start with the cotton. By the time you reach the last cloth, your arms are tired, the sandpaper is clogged with lint, and the light has changed. The last cloth may look worse only because it came last. This is an order effect. To stop it, make the order random. Write each cloth on a paper chit, fold the chits, shake them in a bowl and draw them one by one. A random order does not favour any cloth. For extra care, test each cloth twice, once early and once late. This is why scientists say the order must be random, not 'whatever order feels natural'. Note that a random order may by chance put your favourite first. That is fine. In the long run, no cloth always gets the best slot.
examples: Four chits in a bowl decide which cloth is tested first.
A researcher flips a coin to decide which of two plant pots gets the new fertiliser.
A teacher draws names from a bowl so that no one can guess who is called next.
explanations.art: Four folded chits in a steel bowl, a hand drawing one, and four cloths in a row with the numbers 1 to 4 written beside them in the order drawn.
explanations.context: The order you test things in can quietly change the results. This card explains how a random draw protects a test.

explanations.concept: A test must match the job: wear tests and valid tests
explanations.definition: A valid test measures what you really care about. A wear test rubs a material again and again to see how long it lasts.
explanations.description: A test is valid if it measures what you really care about. Suppose you want to know which cloth lasts longest in a school bag. Pulling one thread until it snaps is easy, but it tells you about threads, not bags. A bag is rubbed against desks, washed, and carried in the rain. So engineers design wear tests that copy this. A wear test rubs a cloth over a rough surface with a fixed push, again and again, and counts the rubs until a hole appears. It is an accelerated test, because it squeezes months of use into minutes. It is also harsher than real life in some ways and kinder in others. It does not include sunlight, sweat or washing. So a wear test answers one question well, and leaves other questions open. Good engineers use several tests, and then check their predictions against real use. Fashion makers, shoe makers and carpet makers all do this.
examples: A shoe-testing machine bends a sole thousands of times to copy months of walking.
A jeans maker rubs the knee of the cloth against a rough wheel and counts rubs until the cloth thins.
A pen maker draws a line on paper with a machine hand, over and over, to see how long the ink lasts.
explanations.art: A cloth stretched over a weighted katori being slid along sandpaper, next to a school bag being rubbed on a bench by a child.
explanations.context: A test can be fair and repeated but still not tell you what you wanted. This card is about tests that copy real life, and what they miss.

explanations.concept: A control: do nothing, and watch
explanations.definition: A control is a sample that gets everything except the thing you are testing.
explanations.description: Sometimes things change by themselves while you are testing. A wet paper strip dries a little. A ball warms up. Ink fades in sunlight. To know what happens anyway, scientists keep a control. A control is a sample that gets everything except the thing you are testing. Say you want to know if rubbing makes a cloth thinner. Keep a piece of the same cloth that is not rubbed, in the same room for the same time. If the untouched piece is also thinner, something else is thinning it. Or say you drop a rubber ball and wonder if the floor matters. Keep one drop from a different, harder floor, but with all else the same. A control is the quiet partner of every fair test. Without it, you may give the credit for a change to the wrong cause.
examples: A strip of cloth in a drawer, while its twin is rubbed, is a control.
A glass of plain water beside the salty water in a floating test is a control.
A plant watered with plain water beside a plant watered with the new plant food.
explanations.art: Two identical cloth squares on a table, one rubbed on sandpaper and one lying untouched under a small card labelled control.
explanations.context: After a test, how do you know your test caused the change? This card explains the sample that does nothing, called a control.

explanations.concept: Why a ball bounces, and why no two bounces are equal
explanations.definition: A ball bounces because it squashes, stores energy, and springs back. Some energy always leaves as sound and warmth.
explanations.description: When a ball hits the floor, it squashes a little. While it squashes, it stores energy, like a squeezed spring. Then it springs back and throws itself up. A bouncier ball is one that stores more of the energy and gives more of it back. But no ball gives back all of it. Some energy becomes sound, the 'thud' you hear. Some becomes a tiny amount of warmth inside the rubber, as its tangled chains rub on each other. That is why each bounce is lower than the last. Now think about why two drops differ. The ball's spin, the exact angle, the spot on the floor, the air and your fingers all change a little. Each tiny change moves the bounce by a tiny amount. We cannot control them all, so we cannot predict one drop exactly. We can only say what usually happens, and how much it varies. Scientists call the fraction of the height that comes back the ball's bounciness, and they find it by dividing the bounce height by the drop height.
examples: A ball that bounces from 50 centimetres to 32 centimetres gives back 32 out of 50, which is about 0.64.
A ball of clay does not bounce, because it keeps its squashed shape and turns the energy into warmth.
A basketball bounces better on a wooden court than on soft sand, because the sand takes the energy.
explanations.art: A rubber ball squashing flat against the floor, with a tiny spring drawn inside it, then jumping up, with small labels for sound and warmth leaving the ball.
explanations.context: We dropped balls and saw different heights. This card explains why a ball bounces at all and why no two bounces are the same.

explanations.concept: Standard tests: so that labs can agree
explanations.definition: A standard test is an agreed recipe. Anyone who follows it should get close to the same answer.
explanations.description: If a company in Chennai says its rope holds 200 kilograms, and a lab in Delhi says it holds 150, who is right? Perhaps both. The company may have pulled slowly, and the lab quickly. It may have been hot or damp. To make results comparable, countries write down standard tests. A standard says exactly how big a sample is, how it is held, how fast it is pulled and in what air. In India, the Bureau of Indian Standards writes many of these. A product that passes its tests may carry the ISI mark. Labs also check each other. Many labs test the same sample and compare numbers. If one lab is far from the rest, it checks its machine. This is the same idea as your two rulers. A test is only useful if other people can repeat it and get close to the same answer.
examples: A helmet that carries the ISI mark has passed fixed tests.
Labs in different countries test the same piece of steel and compare numbers, to check their machines.
A cricket ball must weigh between set limits, so that a ball in Chennai behaves like a ball in Mumbai.
explanations.art: Three different labs in three countries, each pulling a steel bar of the same size, with the same speed written on each test machine.
explanations.context: Two labs can test the same thing and get different numbers. This card explains how standards let people agree.

explanations.concept: Design for the weakest piece, not the average
explanations.definition: A safety factor is how many times stronger than the expected load we make a thing. It covers the weakest piece and surprises.
explanations.description: A lift cable is made of steel strands. Suppose tests on a hundred pieces show a middle value of 20 tonnes before breaking, but a few pieces broke at 14. An engineer will not use 20 as the number to trust. She asks about the weakest pieces and about the worst day. If a cable only ever carries 2 tonnes, she may build it to hold much more than that. This extra strength is the safety factor. It covers unseen cracks, rust, shocks and mistakes. It is also why the spread matters so much. If every piece broke at nearly the same load, a small safety factor would do. If the spread is wide, the factor must be larger. The same idea is used for ropes, chains, bridges and helmets. A fair test finds how far the weakest piece falls below the middle.
examples: A rope sold for 100 kilograms of load may be tested to break above 500 kilograms.
A bridge is built to hold many times the heaviest traffic it will carry.
A climbing rope is retired after a serious fall, even if it looks fine.
explanations.art: A bridge with a tiny car on it and a ghostly row of many heavier lorries drawn faintly on top, showing how much more it could hold.
explanations.context: The weakest piece sets how safe a thing is. This card explains why engineers look at the spread and not just the middle.

explanations.concept: Can a test ever prove that a material is safe?
explanations.description: A test can show that a rope held 500 kilograms ten times. Does that prove it will hold 500 kilograms tomorrow? A rope can fail on the eleventh try. Karl Popper, a philosopher, wrote in 1934 that a test can show a claim is wrong, but can never show it is certainly true. If a thousand swans you see are white, you still cannot be sure that no black swan exists. Engineers and statisticians do not use the word 'prove'. They say how likely a failure is. They say, for example, that fewer than 1 piece in 1,000 will fail at this load. Even this depends on the sample being fair and the future being like the past. Some philosophers say that this is as good as knowing gets. Others say that careful tests build a kind of confidence that deserves to be called knowledge. People still disagree about the best words, but all agree that more tests, more fairness and more honesty make us more sure.
examples: A bridge passes a hundred tests, and engineers still inspect it every year.
Medicines are tested on thousands of people, and doctors still watch for rare effects after sale.
A scientist writes 'the evidence suggests' instead of 'this proves'.

perspectives.explanation: We never say safe for ever. We say how likely a failure is, and we keep inspecting and testing.

perspectives.who: Karl Popper, a philosopher of science
perspectives.explanation: A test can show that a claim is false. It can never show that a claim about all the future is surely true.
We can put a number on how sure we are, for example one failure in a thousand. The number depends on a fair sample.

explanations.art: A row of white swans with one black swan swimming at the edge of the picture, and a question mark above the row.
explanations.context: We keep saying a test makes us more sure. This card asks whether any test can ever make us completely sure.

agreed.text: Repeating the same test gives numbers that are close but not equal.
agreed.evidence: Balls dropped ten times, strips pulled ten times and rice grains measured one by one all show a spread. Labs in every country report the spread along with the middle.

agreed.text: A difference between two materials can be believed only when it is bigger than the ordinary spread within each one.
agreed.evidence: When two ranges overlap, a different set of drops can easily flip the order of the middle values. Scientists check this before they say that one material is better.

agreed.text: Every measuring tool has a smallest step it can show, and some error.
agreed.evidence: Two careful people reading the same ruler often differ by a millimetre or more. Labs check their tools against agreed standards.

agreed.text: A tester who knows which sample is which can be nudged without knowing it, so important tests are done blind.
agreed.evidence: Clever Hans seemed to count until Oskar Pfungst showed in 1907 that the horse followed the questioner's tiny movements. Medicine trials use blind tests for the same reason.

agreed.text: The weakest piece, and not the average, decides how safe a thing is.
agreed.evidence: Cables, ropes and bridges are built several times stronger than the load they will carry, because some pieces are weaker than the middle.

agreed.text: A test answers only the question it was built to ask, so a test must be chosen to match the job.
agreed.evidence: A thread-pulling test says little about how a school bag will wear. Engineers add wear tests and real-life trials.

challenging.claim: The bigger number wins, so a ball that bounced higher once is the bouncier ball.
challenging.for: A bigger number is easy to see and to remember. Sometimes the gap is so big that one try would have shown it.
challenging.against: When the ranges of two balls overlap, a repeat of the test can reverse the order. The ten drops of the rubber ball and the table-tennis ball in the made-up data overlapped almost completely. A fair claim says 'we cannot tell'.
challenging.context: This card is about the shortcut of picking the bigger number from one try.

challenging.claim: Only careless people are fooled by their hopes. A careful scientist is always fair.
challenging.for: Careful people do check their work, and they try to be fair.
challenging.against: Bias works without our knowing. Physicist Richard Feynman said in 1974 that the first rule of science is not to fool yourself, and that you are the easiest person to fool. That is why scientists use blind tests and random order, even when they are sure they are being fair.
challenging.context: This card is about whether being careful is enough to protect a test from our hopes.

challenging.claim: An odd result is a mistake, so throw it away.
challenging.who: Many people when they are in a hurry
challenging.for: Sometimes an odd result really is a slip, such as a coin dropped hard or a strip with a nick.
challenging.against: Sometimes the odd result is the discovery. In 1965, at the DuPont company in the USA, the chemist Stephanie Kwolek made a thin, cloudy liquid that most chemists would have thrown away. She asked for it to be spun into a fibre, and the tests showed the fibre was very stiff and strong for its weight. It became the material called Kevlar. In 1982 the scientist Dan Shechtman saw a pattern in a metal that the textbooks said could not exist. He checked it again and again, many scientists laughed for years, and he won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2011. The rule is to check an odd result, and not to delete it.
challenging.context: This card is about what to do with the one result that does not fit the others.

challenging.for: More tries make the middle value steadier and make luck matter less.
challenging.against: More tries cannot fix a chipped ruler, a hopeful tester or an unfair sample. And after a point, ten more tries add very little. A smarter plan with fewer, fairer tries can beat a hundred careless ones.
challenging.context: This card is about whether piling up repeats is the best way to be sure.

challenging.claim: A good test changes only one thing at a time, and nothing else is fair.
challenging.who: Many school books, and the rule in the Class 3 unit
challenging.for: Changing one thing makes the cause clear. It is the best rule for a beginner.
challenging.against: In 1926 the statistician Ronald Fisher argued that scientists can ask nature several questions at once, if the tests are planned in a careful pattern. Farm trials and factory tests now often change two or three things together, and then work out each one's effect with sums. One at a time is a good rule to start with, but not the only fair one.
challenging.context: This card is about a rule you learned earlier, and a way that expert scientists sometimes go beyond it.

challenging.claim: The test that copies real life is always better than a simple fair test in the kitchen.
challenging.for: A test that copies real use catches problems that a simple test misses, such as sweat on a shoe or wind on a kite.
challenging.against: Real life changes every day, so a real-life trial is hard to compare. A simple test in the kitchen can be repeated ten times and compared fairly. Good testers use both: the fair test to compare, the real-life trial to check.
challenging.context: This card is about the choice between a tidy test and a real-life test.

big_questions.q: One ball, ten drops, ten different heights. What is 'the bounce of the ball'? Is it any single number?
big_questions.hint: Think about the middle value, the range, and whether the ball itself changed between drops.

big_questions.q: If two balls have ranges that overlap almost completely, are they the same ball for every purpose?
big_questions.hint: Think about what 'the same' would mean, and what a longer test or a better ruler might show.

big_questions.q: Richard Feynman said you are the easiest person to fool. Why would that be?
big_questions.hint: Who knows best what you hope for? What do you notice when a result agrees with your guess, and when it does not?

big_questions.q: If the questioner of Clever Hans was not lying, who was fooled, and who was doing the fooling?
big_questions.hint: The questioners nodded without knowing. The horse noticed. Was the horse clever?

big_questions.q: Seeds from the same packet, planted on the same day in the same pot, sprout on different days. Is the spread a problem for life, or something life needs?
big_questions.hint: If every seed sprouted on the same hour, what would happen in a drought?

big_questions.q: A test can show that a rope is weak but cannot show that it will hold for ever. Is there anything in life we can know for sure?
big_questions.hint: Think about the sun rising tomorrow, and how we know it.

big_questions.q: A grandmother can tell a good rope by touch. A test with codes can check her. Which should we trust, and does it need to be one or the other?
big_questions.hint: What does her hand know that a test might miss, and what can a test show that her hand cannot?

big_questions.q: Adverts say 'twice as strong' without saying how many pieces were tested. Is it fair to believe a number with no spread?
big_questions.hint: What would you ask the advert to show you? How many tries? Which ranges?

big_questions.q: Every drop is a little different, so no one can predict exactly where a ball will land. Is the world really exact, with us just unable to see it, or fuzzy at its edges?
big_questions.hint: Scientists disagree about this at the very smallest scale. Think about which tiny causes you could control and which you could not.

big_questions.q: Stephanie Kwolek kept a result that other chemists would have thrown away. How do we decide which odd results to keep?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you could do to find out if an odd result is a slip or a discovery.

how_we_found_out.story: Around 1904 in Berlin, a horse called Clever Hans became famous. His owner, a retired teacher named Wilhelm von Osten, said that Hans could add, subtract and tell the date. Asked a sum, Hans tapped the answer with his hoof. A committee of experts watched and found no trick by the owner. Then a young psychologist, Oskar Pfungst, tried something new. He had people ask questions in secret, without knowing the answer themselves. He also put screens between Hans and the questioner. Hans got the answers wrong. When the questioner knew the answer and Hans could see their face, he was right. Pfungst saw that people made a tiny movement of the head as the taps reached the right number, and Hans stopped there. No one had meant to give a signal. Pfungst published his work in 1907. Since then, scientists test blind, so that nobody can nudge the result by accident.
how_we_found_out.who: Oskar Pfungst, a German psychologist, who tested Clever Hans, the horse of Wilhelm von Osten
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That Hans could do sums, and that if the owner was honest the test must be fair. Pfungst showed that the horse followed tiny, unwitting signals from people who knew the answer. A fair test needs the tester to be in the dark.
how_we_found_out.art: A horse in a Berlin courtyard tapping his hoof, a crowd of people watching, and a young man in a long coat holding a notebook standing behind a screen.

story.title: Ten Pieces of Rope
story.note: A made-up story. Alappuzha (Alleppey) in Kerala is a real centre of coir making, and coir is the fibre of coconut husks. Sree, her family, Jose chettan, the rope company and the numbers of mugs are imagined. The science is real: a single test piece does not show how much pieces vary, the person pouring can nudge the result without knowing, and blind testing with a random order protects against it.
text: Sree lived in Alappuzha, in Kerala, where the backwaters wind between coconut palms. Her family made coir rope. Coir is the rough brown fibre from the husks of coconuts. In the yard behind the house, her mother and aunts spun the fibre into yarn, and the yarn into long ropes that lay across the sand like sleeping snakes.

On a hot Thursday, a man arrived on a scooter, with a shiny bag. His name was Jose, and he came from a rope company in Kochi. Sree's family called him Jose chettan. He put down a coil of bright green rope. 'This is nylon,' he said. 'Twice as strong as coir. I will show you.'

He cut one piece of the green rope and one piece of coir, and hung them from a beam in the shed. To each he tied a steel bucket. Then he filled the buckets with water from the tap, one mug at a time. The coir snapped at nine mugs. The green rope was still holding at twelve, and he stopped. 'You see?' said Jose chettan. 'Twelve against nine.'
Ammamma, Sree's grandmother, had been twisting coir since before Sree's mother was born. She said nothing. But her lips pressed together, and she looked at the broken rope for a long time.
Sree had a teacher at school who said one thing again and again: never trust one drop. One drop of a ball, one pull of a strip, one anything. 'One piece of rope,' said Sree, 'is only one piece.'
Jose chettan laughed kindly. 'A test is a test, child.' But Sree's mother said, 'Let her.' So Sree asked for ten pieces of each rope, all cut to the same length.

They set the first ten pieces in a row. Jose chettan poured the water, mug by mug, and Sree wrote the numbers. After a while Ammamma said, 'You pour the green ones softly, like you are feeding a baby. And you pour the coir ones fast, like you are late for a bus.'
Jose chettan opened his mouth to say no. Then he looked at the notebook, and he closed it again. 'I did not know I did that,' he said slowly.

'Then nobody should know which is which,' said Sree. Her cousin Anu tied a paper tag with a secret letter on each of the twenty pieces. Sree wrote the list of letters in the notebook, folded the page, and put it in her pocket. Then they shook the tags in a steel bowl and drew them, one by one, to decide the order.

Before the first piece was hung, Ammamma took each tagged rope in her hands. She ran the rope between her fingers, and she did not look at the tag. She put two pieces aside. 'These two are poor,' she said. 'I do not know why. They feel thin.'

Now Jose chettan poured, and he did not know whether he was pouring on nylon or coir. He poured every piece the same way, mug after mug, until each snapped. Sree wrote the number for every tag. It took the whole afternoon.

At the end, she opened the folded page. She drew a long line on the floor of the yard with chalk, with numbers from 5 to 15 marked on it. For every rope she put one cashew nut on its number, with the nuts of the same number stacked in a little pile. Coir nuts were brown, and nylon nuts she marked with a dab of green paint.

The pile of brown nuts stood between 7 and 12, with the middle at 9. The green nuts stood between 6 and 14, with the middle at 12 and a half. 'The green rope is stronger in the middle,' said Sree. 'But not every green piece beat every brown piece. One green piece broke at 6. That is lower than any coir.'

Ammamma reached over and touched two nuts. 'These two are the ones I put aside,' she said. One was brown, at 7. The other was green, at 6. They were the two weakest pieces of all twenty. Nobody said anything for a moment. Then Jose chettan smiled and shook his head slowly. 'Your grandmother's hands are a better test than my bucket,' he said.
Sree shook her head. 'Her hands are a test too,' she said. 'But it was the blind test with ten pieces that let us see it. One piece each told us a story that was not true.'

Her mother bought the green rope for the biggest boat, where a snap would be worst. For that rope, she asked Jose chettan to cut her a spare piece from every new coil, so that Ammamma could feel it first. And before any new rope was trusted, Sree tied a ribbon on it, and the family called it 'a rope not yet tested'.
story.epiphany: One piece of rope tells you about one piece. Ten pieces show how much ropes of one kind differ, and the ranges of the two kinds overlap, so 'twice as strong' was too much. The turn comes when the tester is kept in the dark with tags and random order. Then the test is fair, and even Ammamma's hands can be checked.
ask: Why was it not enough to test one piece of each rope?
How did the secret tags make the test fairer?
If the ranges of the two ropes overlap, what can Sree honestly say about which rope is stronger?
Ammamma felt two weak pieces before the test. How could Sree check that she was not just lucky?
Why did Sree tie a ribbon on any rope that had not been tested?

games.title: Real or Luck?
games.context: This is a card game about telling a real difference from ordinary wobble. Each card shows the results of a test with two materials, and you decide whether the difference is real.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a pile in the middle of a table, with two mats on either side, one marked Real and one marked Cannot tell.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the two mats and the pile of cards.

setup.art: A player reading a card aloud while the other players slide a token onto a mat.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Everyone puts a token on a mat.

setup.art: A card turned over to show its back, with the two ranges drawn as bars on a number line.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over and check the ranges.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: results on the front, the answer and the reason on the back

items.f: 1. Ten-drop ball test. The rubber ball gave 31, 33, 30, 34, 32 centimetres of bounce. The marble gave 24, 26, 23, 27, 25 centimetres of bounce. Is the difference real, or can we not tell?
items.b: Real difference. The rubber ball ranged from 30 to 34 and The marble from 23 to 27. The ranges do not touch, so The rubber ball really did give bigger numbers.

items.f: 2. Strip test. Kitchen paper gave 14, 17, 15, 13, 16 coins held. Printer paper gave 15, 18, 16, 19, 17 coins held. Is the difference real, or can we not tell?
items.b: We cannot tell. Kitchen paper ranged from 13 to 17 and Printer paper from 15 to 19. The ranges overlap, so another set of tries could swap the order.

items.f: 3. Stretch test. A thin rubber band gave 12, 14, 13, 15, 12 centimetres of stretch. A thick rubber band gave 22, 24, 23, 25, 21 centimetres of stretch. Is the difference real, or can we not tell?
items.b: Real difference. A thin rubber band ranged from 12 to 15 and A thick rubber band from 21 to 25. The ranges do not touch, so A thick rubber band really did give bigger numbers.

items.f: 4. Soak test. Cotton towel gave 8, 9, 7, 10, 8 millilitres soaked up. Kitchen tissue gave 9, 8, 10, 7, 9 millilitres soaked up. Is the difference real, or can we not tell?
items.b: We cannot tell. Cotton towel ranged from 7 to 10 and Kitchen tissue from 7 to 10. The ranges overlap, so another set of tries could swap the order.

items.f: 5. Umbrella cloth test. Old jeans gave 3, 2, 4, 3, 2 millilitres that came through. A polyester sari gave 8, 9, 7, 10, 8 millilitres that came through. Is the difference real, or can we not tell?
items.b: Real difference. Old jeans ranged from 2 to 4 and A polyester sari from 7 to 10. The ranges do not touch, so A polyester sari really did give bigger numbers.

items.f: 6. Slide test. A steel tray gave 4, 6, 5, 7, 5 seconds to slide down. A plastic tray gave 5, 7, 6, 4, 6 seconds to slide down. Is the difference real, or can we not tell?
items.b: We cannot tell. A steel tray ranged from 4 to 7 and A plastic tray from 4 to 7. The ranges overlap, so another set of tries could swap the order.

items.f: 7. Bag test. A paper bag gave 40, 45, 38, 50, 42 coins held. A jute bag gave 48, 52, 46, 55, 50 coins held. Is the difference real, or can we not tell?
items.b: We cannot tell. A paper bag ranged from 38 to 50 and A jute bag from 46 to 55. The ranges overlap, so another set of tries could swap the order.

items.f: 8. Wear test. Thin cotton gave 20, 25, 18, 22, 21 rubs before a hole. Thick denim gave 60, 66, 58, 70, 63 rubs before a hole. Is the difference real, or can we not tell?
items.b: Real difference. Thin cotton ranged from 18 to 25 and Thick denim from 58 to 70. The ranges do not touch, so Thick denim really did give bigger numbers.

items.f: 9. Bounce test. A table-tennis ball gave 34, 36, 33, 35, 37 centimetres of bounce. A rubber ball gave 33, 35, 32, 36, 34 centimetres of bounce. Is the difference real, or can we not tell?
items.b: We cannot tell. A table-tennis ball ranged from 33 to 37 and A rubber ball from 32 to 36. The ranges overlap, so another set of tries could swap the order.

items.f: 10. Thread test. Cotton thread gave 18, 25, 14, 22, 20 coins held. Polyester thread gave 24, 19, 27, 21, 16 coins held. Is the difference real, or can we not tell?
items.b: We cannot tell. Cotton thread ranged from 14 to 25 and Polyester thread from 16 to 27. The ranges overlap, so another set of tries could swap the order.

items.f: 11. Squash test. A sponge gave 10, 12, 11, 9, 12 millimetres the pad was squashed. A rubber mat gave 2, 3, 2, 3, 4 millimetres the pad was squashed. Is the difference real, or can we not tell?
items.b: Real difference. A sponge ranged from 9 to 12 and A rubber mat from 2 to 4. The ranges do not touch, so A sponge really did give bigger numbers.

items.f: 12. Drying test. A cotton cloth gave 30, 34, 28, 33, 31 minutes to dry. A woollen cloth gave 45, 50, 44, 48, 47 minutes to dry. Is the difference real, or can we not tell?
items.b: Real difference. A cotton cloth ranged from 28 to 34 and A woollen cloth from 44 to 50. The ranges do not touch, so A woollen cloth really did give bigger numbers.

items.f: 13. Pull test. A banana fibre cord gave 22, 30, 17, 26, 24 coins held. A coir cord gave 27, 20, 31, 18, 25 coins held. Is the difference real, or can we not tell?
items.b: We cannot tell. A banana fibre cord ranged from 17 to 30 and A coir cord from 18 to 31. The ranges overlap, so another set of tries could swap the order.

items.f: 14. Soak test. Printer paper gave 5, 6, 4, 5, 6 millilitres soaked up. Kitchen towel gave 14, 13, 15, 12, 14 millilitres soaked up. Is the difference real, or can we not tell?
items.b: Real difference. Printer paper ranged from 4 to 6 and Kitchen towel from 12 to 15. The ranges do not touch, so Kitchen towel really did give bigger numbers.

items.f: 15. Tear test. Newspaper gave 9, 11, 10, 8, 12 coins held. Notebook paper gave 12, 10, 13, 11, 9 coins held. Is the difference real, or can we not tell?
items.b: We cannot tell. Newspaper ranged from 8 to 12 and Notebook paper from 9 to 13. The ranges overlap, so another set of tries could swap the order.

items.f: 16. Bounce test. A small rubber ball gave 44, 42, 46, 43, 45 centimetres of bounce. A hollow plastic ball gave 28, 30, 27, 29, 31 centimetres of bounce. Is the difference real, or can we not tell?
items.b: Real difference. A small rubber ball ranged from 42 to 46 and A hollow plastic ball from 27 to 31. The ranges do not touch, so A small rubber ball really did give bigger numbers.

items.f: 17. Warm-up test. A steel tumbler gave 22, 25, 21, 24, 23 minutes for cold water to warm up. A plastic tumbler gave 24, 26, 23, 27, 25 minutes for cold water to warm up. Is the difference real, or can we not tell?
items.b: We cannot tell. A steel tumbler ranged from 21 to 25 and A plastic tumbler from 23 to 27. The ranges overlap, so another set of tries could swap the order.

items.f: 18. Scratch test. A steel plate gave 2, 3, 2, 3, 2 millimetres of scratch line. A copper plate gave 6, 7, 5, 6, 7 millimetres of scratch line. Is the difference real, or can we not tell?
items.b: Real difference. A steel plate ranged from 2 to 3 and A copper plate from 5 to 7. The ranges do not touch, so A copper plate really did give bigger numbers.

items.f: 19. Only ONE try. A rubber ball bounced to 31 centimetres and a marble bounced to 25 centimetres. Is the difference real?
items.b: We cannot tell yet. One try each shows no spread. Drop each ball ten times before deciding.

items.f: 20. Only TWO tries. Cotton cloth held 12 and 16 coins. Woollen cloth held 15 and 20 coins. Is the difference real?
items.b: We cannot tell yet. Two tries are too few. The ranges 12 to 16 and 15 to 20 already overlap. Test more pieces.

items.f: 21. A tester who hoped for a win drops a rubber ball three times and a marble three times. The results are 30, 31, 32 and 24, 25, 26. Afterwards he admits that he let the rubber ball go from a little higher each time. Can we trust these results?
items.b: Not yet. The ranges do not touch, but the tester may have nudged the result without knowing. Ask a helper to hide the ball names with codes and repeat the test blind.

items.f: 22. A ruler's first centimetre is chipped, so it starts at 1 centimetre. Every reading is 1 centimetre too big. Two ropes read 21 and 24 centimetres of stretch. Is the gap between them changed by the chipped end?
items.b: No. Both readings are too big by the same amount, so the gap between them is the same. The chipped end hurts the true size of each stretch but not the difference.

items.f: 23. The rubber ball bounced 30, 30, 31, 31, 32. The marble bounced 25, 24, 24, 26, 12. Is the marble's 12 something to delete?
items.b: Do not delete it yet. Check what went wrong. Maybe the marble hit the edge of the tile. If so, say so and test again. Even without the 12, the marble's range of 24 to 26 does not touch the rubber ball's range.

items.f: 24. Ten strips of one paper held between 14 and 30 coins. Another paper held between 18 and 22 coins. Which paper is the safer choice for a heavy load?
items.b: The second paper. Its weakest strip held 18 coins, more than the first paper's weakest at 14. The first paper's range is wider. For safety, look at the weakest piece, not the best.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 24 cards and the 8 tokens. 2. Shuffle the cards and put them face down. 3. Give each player one Real token and one Cannot tell token.

flow.context: This is the first step of Real or Luck?, a game about telling a real difference from ordinary wobble.
