games.title: Three Ways to Be Fooled
games.context: This is a sorting game. Each card tells a short story of a test that went wrong, and you decide which of three ways the tester was fooled.

setup.art: Three mats on a floor labelled The thing varies, The measuring is rough, and We hoped for it, with a pile of cards in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Put out the three mats and the pile of cards.

setup.art: A player holding a card and choosing a mat, while another player holds a pencil to score.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card and put it on the mat you think fits best.

setup.art: A card turned over to show an answer and a fix.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over to check, and read the fix.

printables.title: 18 two-sided cards: a short story on the front, the answer and the fix on the back

items.f: 1. Anu dropped a ball once and read 36 centimetres. Her brother dropped it once and read 31. They argued about who was right.
items.b: The thing varies. One drop is only one drop. The fix: drop it ten times and draw a dot plot.

items.f: 2. Ravi wanted the green cloth to win, and he pulled the blue cloth a little faster each time without noticing.
items.b: We hoped for it. The fix: a helper puts secret codes on the cloths and keeps the list until the end.

items.f: 3. A ruler is chipped, so it starts at 1 centimetre. Meena measured every strip with it.
items.b: The measuring is rough. This is a zero error. The fix: check the ruler against another ruler, or subtract 1.

items.f: 4. Two strips cut from the same roll of paper tore at 14 and 19 coins.
items.b: The thing varies. No two strips are exactly the same. The fix: test ten strips from the roll.

items.f: 5. Kavya reads the bounce from far away and from a high chair. Her mother reads it from eye level. They get different numbers.
items.b: The measuring is rough. Where you look from changes what you read. The fix: both read from eye level, or film in slow motion.

items.f: 6. Farhan tested the red cloth first, when his arms were fresh. He tested the blue cloth last, when he was tired.
items.b: We hoped for it, in a quiet way. The order favoured the red cloth. The fix: draw the order from a bowl.

items.f: 7. A kitchen scale moves in steps of 5 grams. Lakshmi tries to tell if a coin weighs 2 grams more than another coin.
items.b: The measuring is rough. The tool's smallest step is bigger than the difference. The fix: use a finer scale, or weigh 10 coins at once.

items.f: 8. Ten grains of the same rice are measured. They are 6.8, 7.1, 6.9, 7.4, 7.0, 6.7, 7.2, 6.9, 7.1 and 7.3 millimetres long.
items.b: The thing varies. Grains of one kind are never the same length. The fix: report the range and the middle value.

items.f: 9. Selvi was told that the new bag was the best. She tested it three times and the old bag only once.
items.b: We hoped for it. She gave the new bag more chances to show a good result. The fix: give both bags the same number of tries.

items.f: 10. A thread breaks at 18 coins on one try and 27 on another.
items.b: The thing varies. Each piece of thread has its own weakest spot. The fix: test many pieces and look at the range.

items.f: 11. The tester reads the ball's bounce as it flashes by. The ball is moving too fast for the eye.
items.b: The measuring is rough. Eyes are slow. The fix: film the bounce on a phone and look at it frame by frame.

items.f: 12. Joseph only wrote down the tries that agreed with his guess, and he forgot the others.
items.b: We hoped for it. He picked results to fit his idea. The fix: write down every try, even the ones you do not like.

items.f: 13. Four paper cups hold different amounts of water before they leak: 180, 195, 170 and 190 millilitres.
items.b: The thing varies. Even cups from one box differ a little. The fix: test many cups and give the range.

items.f: 14. Ishita measured with a cloth tape that has stretched with use.
items.b: The measuring is rough. A stretched tape gives a reading that is too small, the same way each time. The fix: compare it with a rigid ruler.

items.f: 15. A baker is sure the new flour makes better rotis, and she tastes the roti with the new flour first and tells everyone.
items.b: We hoped for it. Her own hopes, and what she told others, could change what they tasted. The fix: serve the rotis to tasters with secret codes.

items.f: 16. The same marble dropped from the same height lands on slightly different spots on the tile.
items.b: The thing varies. A tiny change in spot, spin and angle changes the bounce. The fix: mark the landing square, and drop ten times.

items.f: 17. A thermometer reads 2 degrees too high in every reading.
items.b: The measuring is rough, with a zero error. The fix: check it in ice water, which should read 0.

items.f: 18. A teacher knows which pot got the new plant food, and measures that plant's height more carefully, from the top of the tallest leaf.
items.b: We hoped for it. Her hopes changed how she measured. The fix: the measurer does not know which pot is which.

printables.title: Three mats
items: THE THING VARIES: pieces and tries are never exactly alike
THE MEASURING IS ROUGH: the tool or the reading is not exact
WE HOPED FOR IT: our wish nudged the result

rules: Cut out the 18 cards. Shuffle them and put them face down in a pile.
The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud.
Everyone chooses a mat and points at it. If you cannot agree, vote.
Turn the card over and read the back. A player who chose the right mat wins one token.
A player who says the fix before the card is turned over wins one more token.
Some cards could fit two mats. If the group can give a good reason, the parent decides.
After all the cards, the player with most tokens wins.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the three mats. 2. Shuffle the 18 cards and put them in a pile. 3. Put the tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Each card tells a story of a test that went wrong. There are three ways a test can go wrong. We find which one it was.
flow.kid: Put out the three mats. Shuffle the cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Three Ways to Be Fooled, a sorting game about what can go wrong in a test.

flow.do: Read the three mats aloud. Ask the question below before you play card 1.
flow.say: The three mats are: the thing varies, the measuring is rough and we hoped for it. Can you think of an example for each one?
flow.kid: Read the mats. Think of one example for each.

ask.q: What is one way a test can go wrong that fits each mat?
good: A strip with a hidden nick fits the first mat.
A chipped ruler fits the second mat.
Wanting one cloth to win fits the third mat.

flow.context: In this step, you learn the three mats before the first card.

flow.do: Play cards 1 to 12. Turn each card over after the group has chosen a mat. Read the fix aloud.
flow.say: Read a card. Choose a mat. Then read the back together.
flow.kid: Read a card. Choose a mat. Check the back.

check.q: A tester measures with a ruler whose end is chipped. Which mat fits?
options: The measuring is rough
The thing varies
We hoped for it
check.why: A chipped end gives the same error on every reading. That is a fault in the measuring tool. Choosing 'the thing varies' usually means thinking all wobble comes from the material.

flow.context: In this step, you play the middle of the game and learn a fix for each fault.

flow.do: Play cards 13 to 18. Then count the tokens.
flow.say: Last cards. Then we count tokens.
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Count your tokens.
flow.context: In this step, you finish the cards and count the score.

flow.do: Ask each player to tell one test they did at home. Which mat does the biggest risk in it belong to?
flow.say: Think of one of your own tests. Which mat is the biggest risk for it?
flow.kid: Pick one of your tests. Which mat is its biggest risk?
flow.context: This is the last step of Three Ways to Be Fooled. You use the mats on a real test of your own.

experiments.title: The Bounce Test: ten drops, four balls
experiments.question: If you drop the same ball ten times from the same height, does it bounce to the same height each time? And can ten drops tell you which of four things really bounces highest?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which of the four things will bounce highest, and which lowest? If you drop one ball ten times, will you get the same height every time? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every ball is let go from the same height, with its bottom at the 50 centimetre flag, onto the same square of floor. You let go and do not throw. Two people read each bounce from eye level. The order of the balls is drawn from a bowl, and then reversed, so no ball always goes first or last. Only the ball changes. Then the ten drops of each ball show how much that ball varies, and you can see whether the difference between balls is bigger than the variation.
results_table: Your helper's readings of the same 10 drops (cm)

materials.item: a rubber ball or a cricket-tennis ball that bounces well
a table-tennis ball or any small hollow ball that bounces
a marble (glass or steel)
a ball of modelling clay or crumpled kitchen foil, about as big as the marble or a little bigger
a tailor's tape measure or a long paper strip marked in centimetres, and masking tape
4 folded paper chits, one for each ball, in a small bowl
pencil, paper and a ruler to draw the results table and the dot plot
a phone to film one ball in slow motion (optional)

experiments.safety: Keep marbles away from children under five, and pick up every marble after the test so nobody slips on one.
experiments.record: Draw a table with one row for each ball. Write the ten readings by you, and the ten readings by your helper. Then draw a dot plot with a row for each ball on one number line. Write the range and the middle value of each ball.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you drop four things ten times each from the same height and look at how much the bounces vary. Then you decide which differences between balls are real.

setup.art: A tailor's tape measure taped up a wall with its zero at the floor, a small flag of masking tape at 50 centimetres and a square of tape on the floor below.
setup.caption: 1. Tape the tape measure up the wall. Mark 50 centimetres. Tape a square on the floor.

setup.art: Four paper chits in a steel bowl, with a hand drawing one, and the four balls in a row beside the bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the four chits to set the order of the balls.

setup.art: A child holding a rubber ball with its bottom at the flag, and the ball falling toward the taped square.
setup.caption: 3. Hold the ball with its bottom at the flag, and let go. Do not throw.

setup.art: A child and a parent crouching with their eyes level with the top of the bounce, each with a pencil and paper.
setup.caption: 4. Both of you crouch and read where the ball's bottom reaches at the top of the bounce.

setup.art: A number line from 0 to 60 on paper with a row of dots for each of the four balls.
setup.caption: 5. Draw one dot plot with a row for each ball.

flow.do: Show your child the four things. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess down.
flow.say: We will drop four things from the same height. Which will bounce highest? Which will bounce lowest? If we drop one ball ten times, will it bounce the same each time? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four things to drop. Which bounces highest? Will one ball bounce the same each time? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that thing will bounce highest?
Will one ball bounce to the same height every time? Why?
good: No, because it is hard to drop exactly the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. Write each guess and each reason on paper. The guess about the same height each time matters most, because the experiment is built to test it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bounce Test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Tape the tape measure up a wall, with zero at the floor. 2. Stick a flag of tape at 50 centimetres. 3. Tape a square on the floor below. 4. Fold the four chits and put them in a bowl. 5. Draw the results table.
flow.say: We need a place where every drop is the same. The flag marks the height. The square marks the spot. The bowl will decide the order.
flow.kid: Tape up the measure. Mark the flag and the square.
flow.parent: If the floor is soft, such as carpet or a mat, put a smooth hard board, a ceramic tile or a thick book on the floor under the square. The same hard floor must be used for every ball.

check.q: Why do we tape a square on the floor and let go from the flag every time?
options: So only the ball changes and every drop starts the same
So the floor looks tidy
So the balls cannot roll away
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the height or spot also changed, a difference in the bounce might come from them and not from the ball. Choosing 'looks tidy' misses the point: the tape is a measuring aid.

flow.context: In this step, you build the bounce wall, so every drop starts from the same height and lands on the same spot.

flow.do: Drop the rubber ball three times for practice. Let go with the bottom of the ball at the flag. Crouch so your eyes are level with the top of the bounce.
flow.say: Let go, do not throw. Crouch down. Look at the bottom of the ball when it is highest. Read that number.
flow.kid: Let go. Crouch. Look at the top of the bounce.
flow.parent: Reading a bounce by eye is hard. If you have a phone, film the three practice drops in slow motion next to the tape measure, then play them back. Show your child how the eye misses the highest point.
flow.context: In this step, you practise reading a bounce. It is quick, so you need a few tries.

flow.do: 1. Draw the four chits. That is the order of the balls. 2. Drop each ball once in that order. 3. Then drop each ball once in the reverse order. 4. Both of you write down every reading, without looking at each other's paper. 5. Do this twice.
flow.say: Draw the chits for the order. Drop each ball once. Then go backwards. Write what you see. Do not look at each other's paper.
flow.kid: Draw the order. Drop each ball. Then go backwards. Write the numbers.

ask.q: Is the same ball giving the same number each time?
good: No, the numbers are close but different.

flow.parent: Writing without looking at each other's paper matters. Looking would make the readings agree for the wrong reason. Expect the numbers for one ball to differ by a few centimetres.
flow.context: In this step, you drop each ball four times, in a random order and then in reverse, and both of you write what you read.

flow.do: Keep going until each ball has been dropped ten times. Keep the same method. Draw new chits for the order at the start of every second pair.
flow.say: Ten drops for each ball. Same method, same flag, same square. Keep writing every number, even the odd ones.
flow.kid: Finish ten drops for each ball. Write every number.
flow.parent: If a ball rolls off the square, call it a miss and drop again, but write down that it was a miss. Do not hide misses. The clay ball will not bounce. Write 0 for it every time.
flow.context: In this step, you finish the ten drops. Every number counts, including odd ones.

flow.do: For each drop, find the gap between your reading and your helper's reading. Circle the biggest gap. Talk about why two people read the same bounce differently.
flow.say: Look at your numbers next to your helper's numbers. Where is the biggest gap? Why might two careful people read the same bounce differently?
flow.kid: Compare your numbers with your helper's. Circle the biggest gap.

ask.q: Why did two careful people read the same drop differently?
good: Our eyes were at different heights.
The ball is fast and the top is hard to see.
One of us looked a moment later.

flow.parent: A gap of 1 to 3 centimetres is normal. A gap bigger than that suggests one reader was standing, not crouching.
flow.context: In this step, you compare two sets of readings of the same drops. This shows how rough measuring is.

flow.do: Draw a number line from 0 to 60 across a page. Make a row of dots for each ball, using your readings. Stack equal results. Write the range and the middle value for each ball.
flow.say: Draw the dot plot. One row for each ball. Look at the rows. Which rows overlap? Which rows are far apart?
flow.kid: Draw a dot plot. One row for each ball. Which rows overlap?

ask.q: Which balls have rows that overlap? Which are far apart?
good: The rubber ball and the table-tennis ball overlap.
The clay ball is far from all the others.

flow.parent: Expect the rubber, table-tennis and marble rows to be a few centimetres wide each. Some may overlap and some may not. Both are good results. If your rows are very wide, look at the biggest gaps in step 6 for a hint.
flow.context: In this step, you draw all the drops as dots, so you can see the spread and the overlaps.

flow.do: Write a claim, the evidence and the reasoning for the pair of balls whose rows are closest. Add one sentence that says how sure you are, and why.
flow.say: Pick the two closest balls. Write what you can honestly say about them. Then say how sure you are.
flow.kid: Pick two balls. Write claim, evidence and reasoning. Say how sure you are.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like: Claim: the rubber ball bounces higher than the marble. Evidence: the rubber ball's ten drops ranged from 30 to 35 and the marble's from 23 to 28. Reasoning: the ranges do not touch, so the gap is bigger than the wobble. I am fairly sure, but the test used one floor.

check.q: The rubber ball's ten drops ranged from 30 to 35. The marble's ranged from 23 to 28. Which claim is fair?
options: The rubber ball bounces higher. The ranges do not touch.
We cannot tell, because every drop was a bit different.
The marble bounces higher once in a while.
check.why: The marble's highest drop, 28, is below the rubber ball's lowest, 30. The difference is bigger than the wobble in each ball, so it is a real difference. Choosing 'cannot tell' usually means thinking any wobble at all makes comparing impossible.

flow.context: In this step, you decide which differences are real and which are not, and you write it as a scientist would.

experiments.title: The Secret Code Test: does a label change what we feel?
experiments.question: Do people feel the same cloth as softer when it has a 'Premium' label, and does the score change when they cannot see the label?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will people give the cloth marked Premium a higher softness score than the cloth marked Basic, even though both squares are cut from the same cloth? Will the answer change when people cannot see the labels? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All squares are cut from one piece of cloth, so they are exactly the same. The same people feel them, with clean dry hands, in the same room. A coin toss decides whether a person feels the Premium or Basic square first. You say nothing while people give their scores, so your face and voice cannot help. The only thing that changes between rounds is whether people can see the label.

materials.item: one soft piece of old cotton cloth, such as a towel or a hanky, about 20 centimetres by 20 centimetres
scissors, used by a grown-up
2 small paper labels: one that says 'Premium' with a star drawn in gold or yellow, and one that says 'Basic' written plainly
tape or a rubber band to fix the labels to the squares
a coin for the coin toss
a scarf, or ask people to close their eyes
at least 5 people to feel the squares: the family, grandparents or neighbours
paper and pencil for the table

experiments.safety: Use scissors only with a grown-up. Ask each person if they are happy to take part, and tell everyone the whole truth at the end.
experiments.record: Draw a table with one row for each person. Write each person's scores in both rounds. Work out the difference for each person. Then draw a dot plot of the open-round differences and a dot plot of the blind-round differences on the same number line from minus 5 to plus 5.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you find out whether a label can change what people feel, and whether a blind test can stop it. The cloth is the same in every square.

setup.art: A grown-up cutting four squares of the same soft cotton cloth, each about 8 centimetres wide, and laying them in a row.
setup.caption: 1. Cut four identical squares from the same cloth.

setup.art: Two squares, one with a Premium label with a gold star and one with a plain Basic label, on a plate.
setup.caption: 2. Label one square Premium and one square Basic.

setup.art: A person feeling a square with their eyes shut, while the child holds a coin and a list.
setup.caption: 3. Round 2: the person feels the squares with their eyes shut.

setup.art: A table on paper with a row for each person and columns for the two rounds, with a number line below for the dot plots.
setup.caption: 4. Write the scores and work out the differences.

flow.do: Show your child the cloth. Ask for a guess and a reason. Do not say yet what the test will show.
flow.say: We will ask people how soft two squares feel. One is labelled Premium. One is labelled Basic. Will they say Premium is softer? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two squares. One says Premium. One says Basic. Which will people call softer? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think people will give those scores?
good: The label makes them think it is softer.
They will just feel the cloth and give the same score.

flow.parent: Do not tell your child how the test will turn out, and do not hint. Write the guess and the reason down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Secret Code Test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts four squares from the same cloth. Put a Premium label on one square and a Basic label on a second. Leave two squares plain. Mark them K and M underneath in pencil.
flow.say: The squares are cut from one cloth. They are exactly the same. Two will have labels. Two will have secret letters.
flow.kid: Cut four squares from one cloth. Label two. Mark two with letters.
flow.parent: The two plain squares are for the blind round. Mark their letters on the underside, where people will not see. Keep all four away from other cloth, so people cannot compare them with a different towel.
flow.context: In this step, you make the four squares for the two rounds.

flow.do: Ask the first person to feel both labelled squares. Toss a coin for who goes first. Heads is Premium first. Ask for a softness score from 0 to 10 for each. Write the scores. Say nothing else.
flow.say: Please feel these two squares. Give each one a softness score from 0 to 10. Zero is rough. Ten is very soft.
flow.kid: Toss a coin. Ask for two scores from 0 to 10. Say nothing else.
flow.parent: Do not smile, nod or say anything while the person is scoring. If you react, your face may tell them which score you hoped for. Repeat with every person. Use the same words for each person.

check.q: Why do we toss a coin to decide which square goes first?
options: So the order does not always favour one square
So the person feels lucky
So the test takes longer
check.why: If Premium always went first, a person might give a higher score just because fresh fingers feel more. A coin toss is a random order. Choosing 'feels lucky' misses the purpose.

flow.context: In this step, you run the open round. Each person sees the labels.

flow.do: Now ask each person to close their eyes or wear the scarf. Hand over the squares marked K and M, one after the other. Toss a coin for the order. Ask for a score for each. Write the scores by the letters.
flow.say: Close your eyes please. Feel this square, then this one. Give each a softness score from 0 to 10.
flow.kid: Eyes closed. Hand over the K and M squares. Write the scores.
flow.parent: Keep a record of which square, K or M, went first. Do not tell anybody what you expect.
flow.context: In this step, you run the blind round. Nobody can see a label.

flow.do: Tell everyone the whole truth. All four squares came from the same cloth. Thank them for helping. Ask them what they thought was happening.
flow.say: Now the secret. All four squares were cut from the same cloth. Did anyone guess? What did you think you felt?
flow.kid: Tell everyone the secret. All four squares are the same.

ask.q: What did you think you felt when you saw the labels?

flow.parent: Be kind. No one was foolish. Even expert tasters are moved by labels.
flow.context: In this step, you tell everyone the truth and thank them.

flow.do: For each person, work out 'Premium minus Basic' for the open round, and 'first minus second' for the blind round. Draw both rows of differences as dots on one number line from minus 5 to plus 5.
flow.say: Take each person's Premium score and subtract the Basic score. Do the same for the blind round. Plot the dots. Where do they sit?
flow.kid: Work out the differences. Plot two rows of dots.

ask.q: What do you notice about the two rows of dots?
good: The open round dots sit mostly above zero.
Both rows are all over the place.
The blind round dots sit around zero.

flow.parent: Be honest about what you see. With five people, the dots may be messy. If the open round sits mostly above zero and the blind round is spread around zero, the label pushed the scores. If both rows look alike, you have found no push. Both results are fine. Do not delete anyone's score.
flow.context: In this step, you turn the scores into differences and draw them, so you can see whether labels made a push.

experiments.title: The Rub Test: which cloth wears through first?
experiments.question: Which of four cloths wears through first when rubbed on sandpaper with the same push, and is the difference bigger than the wobble between two runs of the same cloth?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which cloth will wear through in the fewest rubs, and which will last longest? How many rubs do you think the longest will take? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each cloth is stretched over the flat bottom of the same steel katori with the same weight inside. It is slid the same 20 centimetres along the sandpaper, and back, at the same speed. Each run uses a fresh lane of sandpaper, so lint from one cloth does not change the next run. The order of the cloths is drawn from a bowl. Each cloth is run twice. Only the cloth changes.
results_table: Rubs until the first hole, run 1
Rubs until the first hole, run 2
Smaller and bigger of the two runs
What the cloth looked like at the end

materials.item: 4 pieces of old cloth, each about 12 centimetres square, and two for each cloth: a cotton hanky or old shirt, old jeans, polyester such as an old dupatta, and a kitchen duster
a sheet of coarse sandpaper, labelled 60 to 100, about A4 size
a flat-bottomed steel katori, about 7 centimetres wide
30 one-rupee coins or a small packet of rice, to put in the katori as weight
a strong rubber band or a hair band to hold the cloth on the katori
masking tape and a pencil to draw 8 lanes on the sandpaper and a 20 centimetre guide
4 paper chits and a bowl, to draw the order
a damp cloth to wipe up dust, and newspaper for under the sandpaper
scissors, used by a grown-up, to cut the cloth squares

experiments.safety: Do this on a table covered with newspaper. Rub gently on the sandpaper only, never on skin. Do not blow the dust. Wipe up the dust with a damp cloth when you finish, and wash your hands. A grown-up should cut the cloth and handle the sandpaper edges.
experiments.record: Write the number of rubs until the first hole for every run, or '100 or more' if no hole appeared. Then draw a dot plot with a row for each cloth. Work out the range for each cloth.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you make a small rubbing machine from a katori and sandpaper, and you count how many rubs each cloth takes to wear through. It is a wear test.

setup.art: A sheet of sandpaper taped to a table with eight lanes drawn on it in pencil, each 20 centimetres long, and a chit bowl beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Tape the sandpaper down. Draw eight lanes, each 20 centimetres long.

setup.art: A steel katori upside down with a cloth stretched over its flat bottom, held by a rubber band, and coins in the dish above.
setup.caption: 2. Stretch a cloth over the katori's flat bottom. Hold it with a rubber band.

setup.art: A child sliding the katori along a lane on the sandpaper and back, counting aloud.
setup.caption: 3. Slide the katori along one lane and back. That is one rub.

setup.art: A cloth held up to a window, with one tiny point of light shining through.
setup.caption: 4. Every ten rubs, hold the cloth up to the window. Look for a point of light.

flow.do: Show your child the four cloths. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess down.
flow.say: We will rub four cloths on sandpaper until they wear through. Which will wear through first? Which will last longest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four cloths. Which wears out first? Which lasts longest? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that cloth will last longest?
What would the real life use of the cloth be?

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. Write each guess and the reason.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rub Test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Tape the sandpaper flat to the table. 2. Draw eight lanes, each 20 centimetres long. 3. Number them 1 to 8. 4. Put the coins in the katori. 5. Cut two squares of each cloth.
flow.say: We are building a rubbing machine. The sandpaper is the rough road. The katori with coins is the weight. Each lane is used only once.
flow.kid: Tape down the sandpaper. Draw eight lanes. Number them.
flow.parent: The sandpaper clogs with lint, so a used lane rubs more gently. That is why each run gets a new lane. Choose the loading so that a thin cloth wears through in under 100 rubs. A katori with 30 coins is a good start.
flow.context: In this step, you build the rubbing machine. Eight lanes mean every run starts with fresh sandpaper.

flow.do: Fix a square of cotton over the flat bottom of the katori. Hold it with a rubber band. Check that the cloth is tight and has no wrinkles.
flow.say: Pull the cloth tight. A loose cloth will wrinkle and wear unfairly. Smooth it with your hand.
flow.kid: Stretch the cloth tight. Fix it with a rubber band.

check.q: Why must every cloth be pulled tight in the same way?
options: A loose cloth wrinkles and wears in a different way, so the cloth is not the only thing that changed
A tight cloth looks nicer
It makes the katori heavier
check.why: If one cloth is loose and another is tight, a difference in the rubs might come from the tightness. Only the cloth should change. Choosing 'looks nicer' misses that this is a fair-test step.

flow.context: In this step, you dress the katori with a cloth. A tight cloth gives a fair test.

flow.do: Draw the four chits. That is the order of the cloths for the first round. Write the order down. Practise one rub on an old piece of sandpaper, counting 'one-two' for the way there and back.
flow.say: Draw the order. Then practise one rub. Slide there, slide back. Count one-two. Keep the same speed.
flow.kid: Draw the order. Practise one rub. Count one-two.
flow.parent: The speed matters. A steady count of one second each way is easy to keep. Use a clock with a second hand, or sing a steady beat. Do not press down. Let the weight do the work.
flow.context: In this step, you draw the order and practise a steady speed.

flow.do: Run each cloth in the drawn order, in a fresh lane. Slide the katori to the end of the lane and back for each rub. Count the rubs aloud. Every ten rubs, stop and hold the cloth up to the window. Look for a point of light. Stop at the first hole, or at 100 rubs.
flow.say: One rub is there and back. Count out loud. Every ten rubs, hold the cloth up to the light. A tiny point of light means a hole. Write the number.
flow.kid: Slide there and back. Count. Every ten rubs, look for light.

ask.q: Which cloth is going to last longest, now that you have watched?

flow.parent: If no cloth has a hole after 100 rubs, write '100 or more'. If every cloth lasts to 100, add 20 coins, or use a rougher sandpaper, and start again in new lanes. Note that the loading changed.
flow.context: In this step, you run the first round. Each cloth gets one run in a fresh lane.

flow.do: Run a second round. Draw the chits again for a new order. Use fresh lanes and new squares of cloth. Write the numbers for the second run.
flow.say: Run every cloth a second time. Draw a new order. Use new lanes.
flow.kid: Run a second round. Draw a new order. Use new lanes.
flow.parent: If a second run is very different from the first, do not be surprised. Cloth is not the same everywhere. Write both.
flow.context: In this step, you run the second round. Two runs of each cloth show how much the same cloth varies.

flow.do: Draw a dot plot with a row for each cloth, using both runs. Work out the range. Circle any cloth where the two runs are far apart. Write a claim, evidence and reasoning, and say how sure you are.
flow.say: Draw the dot plot. Which cloth lasted longest? Is the gap bigger than the wobble between its two runs?
flow.kid: Draw a dot plot. Which cloth lasted longest? Say how sure you are.

ask.q: Is the winner clear, or do two cloths overlap?
What does this test leave out about real life?

flow.parent: With only two runs per cloth, many pairs will overlap, and that is a good result to talk about. Ask: how many more runs would you want before you told a friend which cloth to buy?
flow.context: In this step, you draw the results and write what you can honestly say.

activities.title: Two Rulers, One Strip: how rough is our measuring?

materials.item: a strip of paper about 25 centimetres long and 2 centimetres wide
a school ruler
a tailor's cloth tape measure
a second strip of stiff paper for making a home-made ruler
a pencil, tape and a helper

schedule.what: Measure one strip with three tools. Make a ruler with a zero error on purpose. Find the error. Draw the results.

activities.record: A table with the name of each tool and the readings by you and your helper. A short note on which tool had the widest spread and which tool had a zero error.
activities.context: In this activity, you measure the same strip with three different tools, and you find out how rough measuring is. You also make a ruler with a fault on purpose.

setup.art: A paper strip lying beside a school ruler, a tailor's tape and a home-made ruler, with a child and a helper each holding a pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Measure the strip with each tool.

setup.art: A home-made paper ruler drawn with its zero mark half a centimetre in from the end, with a small red arrow pointing at the gap.
setup.caption: 2. Make a ruler whose zero is in the wrong place.

setup.art: A home-made ruler laid beside a school ruler, with the marks lined up and the gap marked between the two zeros.
setup.caption: 3. Compare the home-made ruler with the school ruler to find its zero error.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess how long the strip is to the nearest centimetre. Then both of you measure it with the school ruler, one at a time, without looking at each other's number.
flow.say: How long is the strip? Measure it with the ruler. Do not look at your helper's number. Write what you read.
flow.kid: Measure the strip. Do not peek. Write your number.

ask.q: Did you and your helper get the same number?
good: No, they differed by a millimetre or two.

flow.parent: A difference of 1 to 2 millimetres is normal. Write both numbers. Do not agree on one until later.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Rulers, One Strip. You measure the strip with the school ruler.

flow.do: Repeat the measuring with the tailor's tape. Pull the tape flat but not tight. Write down both readings again.
flow.say: Measure the strip again with the cloth tape. Lay it flat. Do not pull it tight. Write your number.
flow.kid: Measure with the cloth tape. Write your number.
flow.context: In this step, you measure the same strip with a second tool, the cloth tape.

flow.do: Make a paper ruler on stiff paper with a school ruler, marking each centimetre. Start the zero mark half a centimetre in from the end of the paper. Mark the ruler 'home-made'.
flow.say: Draw a ruler on stiff paper. Make a mark for every centimetre. But start your zero half a centimetre from the end. This is a ruler with a fault.
flow.kid: Draw a ruler. Put the zero half a centimetre from the end.
flow.parent: The aim is a ruler that reads wrong in the same way every time. Do not tell the helper where the zero is. Ask the helper to measure the strip with the home-made ruler.
flow.context: In this step, you make a ruler with a zero error on purpose, so you can find a fault like it later.

flow.do: Ask your helper to measure the strip with the home-made ruler, starting from the end of the paper. Write down the reading and compare it with the school ruler.
flow.say: Measure the strip with the home-made ruler. Start at the end of the paper. Is your number the same as before?
flow.kid: Measure with the home-made ruler. Is the number different?

check.q: The home-made ruler reads 0.5 centimetres too much on every strip. You measure two strips and get 12.5 and 17.5 centimetres. How much longer is the second strip really?
options: 5 centimetres, because the error is the same for both
4.5 centimetres, because of the error
5.5 centimetres, because of the error
check.why: The ruler adds 0.5 to both strips. The gap between the two readings is 17.5 minus 12.5, which is 5 centimetres. The zero error cancels out in a difference. Choosing 4.5 or 5.5 usually means subtracting or adding the error again by mistake.

flow.context: In this step, you use the faulty ruler and see how a zero error changes every reading.

flow.do: Lay the home-made ruler beside the school ruler with the centimetre marks lined up. Find the zero error. Write it. This is calibrating.
flow.say: Put the two rulers side by side. Line up the marks. Where does the home-made zero sit? That gap is the zero error.
flow.kid: Line up the rulers. Find the gap between the zeros.

ask.q: Which tool had the biggest gap between you and your helper? Which tool had a zero error?
good: The cloth tape had the biggest gap.
The home-made ruler had a zero error.

flow.context: In this step, you calibrate the faulty ruler against a good one and find its zero error.

activities.title: Rice Lengths: are two kinds of rice really different?

materials.item: a spoonful of basmati rice, or any long-grain rice
a spoonful of ponni rice, idli rice or any short-grain rice
a second spoonful from the same packet of the short-grain rice, as a control
a school ruler marked in millimetres
a plate, a pencil, paper and a strip of tape

schedule.what: Measure 20 grains of each of three samples. Draw three dot plots. Compare the ranges.

activities.record: A table of 20 lengths for each of the three samples in millimetres, three dot plots on one number line, and the range and the middle value of each.
activities.context: In this activity, you measure the length of 20 grains from three spoonfuls of rice. You find out whether two kinds of rice really differ, and how much two spoonfuls of the same rice differ.

setup.art: Three small piles of rice on a plate, labelled A, B and C, with a ruler laid beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Make three piles of 20 grains each.

setup.art: One rice grain laid on a strip of sticky tape beside a millimetre ruler, with the length being read.
setup.caption: 2. Lay each grain on the ruler and read its length to the nearest millimetre.

setup.art: Three rows of dots on one number line from 4 to 10 millimetres, one for each pile.
setup.caption: 3. Draw all the lengths as dots on one number line.

flow.do: Count out 20 grains of long rice for pile A. Count out 20 grains of short rice for pile B. Take 20 more grains from the same packet for pile C. Ask your child to guess the middle length of each pile.
flow.say: Pile A is long rice. Pile B and pile C are both short rice from the same packet. Guess the usual length of a grain in each pile. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Count 20 grains for each pile. Guess a length for each.

ask.q: Will piles B and C be the same? Why do you think so?
good: Yes, because they are from the same packet.
No, because grains are not all the same.

flow.parent: Do not tell your child that B and C are the same rice before the guess. The point is to see how much the same rice varies.
flow.context: This is the first step of Rice Lengths. You make three piles and guess before you measure.

flow.do: Lay each grain against a millimetre ruler. Read the length to the nearest millimetre. A strip of tape on the ruler keeps the grain still. Write each length in the table.
flow.say: Hold the grain still. Look straight down at the ruler. Read the length to the nearest millimetre. Write it down.
flow.kid: Measure each grain. Write its length in millimetres.
flow.parent: Broken grains give odd results. Keep them, but write 'broken'. Reading to the nearest half-millimetre is possible if your eyes are sharp. Two children can share the measuring.
flow.context: In this step, you measure all sixty grains. Take your time, and look straight down at the ruler.

flow.do: Draw a number line from 4 to 10 millimetres. Make a row of dots for each pile. Mark the range of each pile with a bracket. Find the middle value of each.
flow.say: Draw one number line. Make three rows of dots. Which rows overlap? Which row is on its own?
flow.kid: Draw three rows of dots on one number line.

ask.q: Do piles B and C overlap? Does either overlap with pile A?
good: B and C overlap almost completely.
A is far from B and C.

check.q: Piles B and C are two spoonfuls of the same rice from the same packet. Their middle values differ by 0.2 millimetres. What does that tell you?
options: Even the same rice shows a small difference by chance, so a gap this small is not a real difference between kinds
B and C must be different kinds of rice
The ruler is broken
check.why: B and C were meant to be the same. Their small gap shows how big the gap by chance can be. A real difference between rice kinds should be much bigger than that. Choosing 'different kinds' usually means ignoring that two spoonfuls of the same rice can differ.

flow.context: In this step, you draw the lengths as dots, so you can compare the piles at a glance.

flow.do: Ask your child to write a claim, evidence and reasoning about A and B. Then ask them to say why the control, pile C, was useful.
flow.say: Write a claim about the long rice and the short rice. Give your evidence and reasoning. Why did we measure a second spoonful of the short rice?
flow.kid: Write a claim about A and B. Why was pile C useful?
flow.parent: A good claim may be: the long rice is longer than the short rice, because the ranges do not touch. The control tells us how big a gap can be by chance alone.
flow.context: In this step, you write what you can honestly say about the two kinds of rice.

activities.title: The Eight Matchboxes: is your hand better than luck?

materials.item: 8 matchboxes or small identical boxes
20 one-rupee coins, or dry rice in spoons
a bowl, 4 red paper slips and 4 blue paper slips
paper and pencil for the results
a helper who fills the boxes and does not tell
a screen, such as a book standing up or a cloth over a chair

schedule.what: A helper fills 4 boxes with 6 coins and 4 boxes with 4 coins. You sort them by feel. Repeat 5 times. Then compare with pure luck.

activities.record: A table with five rounds. For each round, how many of the four heavy boxes you found. A second row for five rounds of luck, drawn from the bowl of slips. Two dot plots on one number line from 0 to 4.
activities.context: In this activity, you test your own hands as a measuring tool. Can they tell a heavy box from a light box better than blind luck?

setup.art: Eight identical matchboxes in two rows, four with coins inside and four with fewer coins, with a helper filling them behind a screen.
setup.caption: 1. A helper fills 4 boxes with more coins and 4 with fewer. Shuffle.

setup.art: A child holding two boxes, one in each hand, then putting boxes into two piles marked Heavy and Light.
setup.caption: 2. Feel each box. Sort them into two piles of four.

setup.art: A bowl with four red slips and four blue slips, and a hand drawing four slips.
setup.caption: 3. For luck, draw four slips from the bowl and count the red ones.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess how many of the four heavy boxes they will find. Explain only the rules: four boxes are heavy, four are light, and the child must put four in each pile.
flow.say: Four boxes are heavy and four are light. You sort them by feel into two piles of four. How many of the four heavy ones will you find? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four heavy, four light. Sort by feel. How many will you find? Why?

ask.q: What is the chance of getting all four right just by luck? Is it likely?

flow.parent: If a child asks about luck, say we will find out. Do not give the numbers yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Eight Matchboxes. You guess before you test.

flow.do: The helper puts 6 coins in four boxes and 4 coins in the other four boxes. The helper shuffles them behind a screen and places them in a row. The helper writes down which are which and keeps it secret.
flow.say: The helper puts coins in the boxes and mixes them. Nobody else knows which are heavy.
flow.kid: Helper: fill the boxes and mix them. Keep the list secret.
flow.parent: Take all the coins from the table before the child sorts. If the sorting is too easy, make the difference 1 coin. If it is impossible, make it 4 coins.
flow.context: In this step, the helper prepares the boxes, so that the sorter cannot know which is which.

flow.do: Round 1. Your child feels each box and sorts them into a Heavy pile of four and a Light pile of four. The helper counts how many heavy boxes were found, without saying which. Repeat for five rounds, re-shuffling each time.
flow.say: Feel each box. Sort them into Heavy and Light, four in each pile. Then the helper counts how many heavy boxes you found.
flow.kid: Feel each box. Make a Heavy pile and a Light pile.
flow.parent: Do not tell the child which boxes were right until all five rounds are finished. Telling them would help them learn, and it would not be a test.
flow.context: In this step, you sort the boxes five times, and the helper writes down how many heavy boxes you found each time.

flow.do: Now simulate pure luck. Put 4 red and 4 blue slips in a bowl. Draw 4 slips without looking. Count the red ones. Do this ten times, putting the slips back each time. Write down the ten counts.
flow.say: Now we find out what luck gives. Draw four slips from the bowl. Count the red ones. Put them back. Do it ten times.
flow.kid: Draw four slips. Count the red ones. Do it ten times.

ask.q: How often did luck give 4 out of 4?

flow.context: In this step, you find out what pure luck gives, so you can compare it with your hands.

flow.do: Draw both sets of counts as dots on one number line from 0 to 4. Use one row for your hands and one for luck. Ask your child to say whether their hands beat luck, and how sure they are.
flow.say: Draw two rows of dots. One for your hands and one for luck. Do your hands do better? How sure are you?
flow.kid: Draw two rows of dots. Do your hands beat luck?
flow.parent: With only five rounds, your result may look like luck even if your hands are good. Say so. More rounds would help.

check.q: In pure luck, which count is the most common for the number of heavy boxes found among four?
check.why: There are 70 ways to pick 4 boxes out of 8. Of these, 36 give exactly 2 right. Only 1 gives all 4 right. So luck usually gives about 2. Choosing 4 usually means thinking a correct guess is easy.

flow.context: In this step, you compare your hands with luck. A result near the luck row means you are no better than guessing.

activities.title: Claim Detective: how was that number made?

materials.item: 3 or 4 labels, boxes or adverts that make a claim about a material, such as 'twice as strong' or 'absorbs 10 times more'
paper and pencil, and a table drawn with six columns

schedule.what: Collect claims. Ask six questions about each. Choose one claim you could test at home.

activities.record: A table with a row for each claim and a column for each of the six questions. A note on the claim you could test at home.
activities.context: In this activity, you read claims on labels and adverts as a detective. You ask how the number was made, and you decide which claim you could test at home.

setup.art: A kitchen table with three packets and an advert page, each with a claim circled in red.
setup.caption: 1. Collect claims from packets and adverts.

setup.art: A table on paper with six columns: compared with what, how many tries, how big the wobble was, who tested, what was left out, what I could test.
setup.caption: 2. Ask six questions about each claim.

flow.do: Collect three or four claims from packets, labels or adverts at home. If you cannot find any, use these: 'twice as strong', 'absorbs 10 times more' and 'unbreakable'. Write each one at the top of a row.
flow.say: Look for claims about materials on packets and adverts. Words like stronger, softer or longer lasting. Write each claim on its own row.
flow.kid: Find three claims on packets. Write them in your table.
flow.context: This is the first step of Claim Detective. You collect the claims.

flow.do: For each claim, ask six questions: Compared with what? How many tries? How big was the wobble? Who did the test? What did the test leave out? What could I test at home? Write what you can find, or write 'not said'.
flow.say: Ask six questions about each claim. If the packet does not say, write not said. How many times did you write not said?
flow.kid: Ask six questions about each claim. Write not said if unknown.

ask.q: What was most often missing?

flow.parent: Do not tell your child that the claim is false. A claim with 'not said' answers is not shown to be wrong. It is just not shown to be right.
flow.context: In this step, you ask how the claim's number was made. Most claims leave many answers out.

flow.do: Ask your child to pick one claim they could test at home. Plan the test in one line: what changes, what stays the same, what is measured, and how many tries.
flow.say: Pick one claim you could test at home. Write one line: what you change, what you keep the same, and what you measure.
flow.kid: Pick one claim. Plan its test in one line.

check.q: A packet says 'stronger by 30 per cent'. What is the most important missing information?
options: Stronger than what, tested how many times, and with how much wobble
The colour of the packet
The price
check.why: A percentage means nothing without a comparison and a sense of the wobble. If the wobble is bigger than 30 per cent, the claim may be luck. Choosing the price usually means shifting from 'is it true?' to 'is it cheap?'.

flow.context: In this step, you plan a test for one claim, ready for the Family Test Report project.

activities.title: Keep or Chuck? Six odd results

materials.item: paper and pencil
the dot plots from the Bounce Test, if you did it

schedule.what: Read six cases. Decide for each whether to keep the odd result, test again, or explain it. Then look for an odd result in your own data.

activities.record: A table with the six cases and your decision, with one sentence of reasoning for each.
activities.context: In this activity, you read six cases of an odd result, and you decide what a scientist should do in each case. You also look for an odd result in your own Bounce Test data.

setup.art: Six small cards in two rows, each with a short test story and a red dot on one number that does not fit the rest.
setup.caption: 1. Read the six cases.

setup.art: A notebook page with three boxes for each case: keep, test again or explain.
setup.caption: 2. Decide what to do with each odd result.

flow.do: Read cases 1 to 3 aloud. Case 1: a strip held 14, 15 and 3 coins, and the 3-coin strip had a nick. Case 2: a marble bounced 25, 24, 26 and 12, and you saw it hit the edge of a tile. Case 3: a rubber ball bounced 30, 31, 32 and 45, and you saw nothing special.
flow.say: Read each case. What would you do with the odd number? Keep it, test again, or explain it?
flow.kid: Read three cases. What do you do with each odd number?

ask.q: What would you do in case 3, where nothing seems wrong?
good: Keep it and look for the cause.

flow.parent: Case 1 has a known cause: explain it, keep a note, test again. Case 2 has a known cause too. Case 3 has no known cause, so test again and do not delete the 45 in secret.
flow.context: This is the first step of Keep or Chuck. You read the first three cases.

flow.do: Read cases 4 to 6 aloud. Case 4: in 1965 a chemist made a cloudy, thin liquid that others would throw away. She had it spun anyway. Case 5: a fifth strip held 80 coins when the others held 20, because the helper added coins by mistake. Case 6: a cloth lasted 20 rubs one time and 90 the next, with no known reason.
flow.say: Read the last three cases. Which odd results are mistakes? Which could be discoveries?
flow.kid: Read three more cases. Mistake or discovery?

ask.q: How can you tell a mistake from a discovery?
good: You cannot tell by looking. You have to test again.
Check what went wrong and repeat.

flow.parent: In case 4, say that the chemist was Stephanie Kwolek, and the fibre became Kevlar. Not every odd result is a discovery. The scientist's skill is to check it, not delete it or believe it at once.
flow.context: In this step, you read the last three cases, including a real one about the chemist Stephanie Kwolek.

flow.do: Ask your child to write a rule for odd results in one sentence. Then look at the dot plots from the Bounce Test, or any other data, and find one result that looks odd.
flow.say: Write one rule for odd results. Then look at your own data. Is there a dot that stands away from the rest?
flow.kid: Write a rule for odd results. Find one odd dot in your data.

check.q: A strip held 14, 15, 14 and 3 coins. The 3 is odd. What is the best next step?
options: Check the strip for a nick, write down what you find, and test again
Delete the 3 because it does not fit
Change the 3 to 14 to match the rest
check.why: An odd result has a cause, and finding the cause is part of the work. Deleting or changing a result hides evidence. Choosing 'delete' usually means wanting a tidy table more than the truth.

flow.context: In this step, you write your own rule and look for an odd result of your own.

flow.do: Share the rule you wrote. Ask what a scientist loses if she deletes every odd result.
flow.say: Read out your rule. What might a scientist lose if she deletes every odd result?
flow.kid: Read your rule aloud.
flow.context: In this step, you share your rule and talk about what is at risk.

activities.title: Wet or Dry? Does the strongest paper stay the strongest?

materials.item: strips 2 centimetres wide and 20 centimetres long, cut from kitchen towel, printer paper, newspaper and tissue paper: 2 strips of each
2 clothes pegs, a pencil, 2 piles of books or 2 chair backs
a small paper cup or plastic katori, thread and a medicine cup or measuring cup marked in millilitres
a jug of water, a plate and a towel for drips
scissors and a ruler, to cut the strips
paper and pencil

schedule.what: Test each paper dry and wet. Pour water into a hanging cup until the strip tears. Measure the water. Compare the ranking dry and wet.

activities.record: A table with a row for each paper, the millilitres of water the dry strip held and the millilitres the wet strip held. A ranking for dry and a ranking for wet.
activities.context: In this activity, you test four papers dry and wet, using water in a hanging cup as the load. You find out whether the strongest paper stays the strongest when it is wet.

setup.art: A paper strip clipped at the top to a peg hanging from a pencil on two piles of books, and a small cup hanging from a peg at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Hang a strip and a cup.

setup.art: A hand pouring water slowly from a jug into the hanging cup, with the strip stretching.
setup.caption: 2. Pour water into the cup until the strip tears.

setup.art: The torn cup's water being poured into a medicine cup to read the millilitres.
setup.caption: 3. Measure the water in the cup.

flow.do: Show your child the four papers. Ask for a guess and a reason. Which paper will hold the most when dry? Which when wet? Will the order change?
flow.say: Four papers. Dry and wet. Which holds most when dry? Which holds most when wet? Will the order change? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four papers. Dry and wet. Will the order change? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think wetting will change the order?
good: Some papers are made to survive water.

flow.context: This is the first step of Wet or Dry. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Rest the pencil on two piles of books. 2. Clip one strip in a peg and hang the peg on the pencil. 3. Clip a second peg at the bottom of the strip. 4. Tie a thread from the second peg to a light cup.
flow.say: We hang a strip from a pencil. At the bottom, a cup hangs on a thread. We will pour water into the cup slowly.
flow.kid: Hang the strip. Hang a cup below it.
flow.parent: The cup should hang about 20 centimetres above the floor. Put a tray or plate under it. Check that the strip is straight and not nicked.
flow.context: In this step, you build the testing rig. The pegs hold the strip.

flow.do: Draw four chits for the order. For each paper, test one dry strip. Dip a second strip in water for 10 seconds. Let it drip for 5 seconds. Then test it wet. Pour water slowly, in a steady stream, until the strip tears. Measure the water in the cup.
flow.say: Pour slowly and steadily into the cup. Stop when the strip tears. Pour the water in the cup into the medicine cup. Write the millilitres.
flow.kid: Pour slowly. Stop when it tears. Measure the water.
flow.parent: A wet strip may tear at the peg. If it slips out, note it and try a new strip. Tissue paper may tear very early, with only a spoon of water.
flow.context: In this step, you test each paper dry and wet. One millilitre of water weighs about one gram.

flow.do: Rank the papers from strongest to weakest, once for dry and once for wet. Draw the two rankings side by side.
flow.say: Rank the papers for dry. Rank them again for wet. Did the order change?
flow.kid: Rank the papers dry and wet. Did the order change?

ask.q: Which paper changed the most when wet?

check.q: A paper bag for rainy days: which test should you trust?
options: The wet test, because rain makes bags wet
The dry test, because it is easier
Either, because strong is strong
check.why: A test is valid when it copies the real job. A bag in the rain is wet. A dry test says little about wet use. Choosing 'strong is strong' usually means thinking a material has one strength.

flow.context: In this step, you rank the papers twice and compare.

flow.do: Write a claim, evidence and reasoning. Add one sentence about how sure you are, given that you tested only two strips of each.
flow.say: Write your claim. Say how sure you are when you tested only two strips of each paper.
flow.kid: Write your claim. Say how sure you are.
flow.context: In this step, you write your result honestly, with its limits.

projects.title: Our Family Test Report: a claim, tested properly

materials.item: a claim you chose in Claim Detective, such as 'this bag holds more' or 'this tissue is stronger'
at least 10 pieces of each of two things to compare
secret code labels: small paper tags marked with letters, a helper, a bowl for drawing the order
a measuring tool such as a medicine cup, a ruler or coins
paper and pencil, and a large sheet for the report

schedule.what: Choose the claim. Plan what changes, what stays the same and what is measured. Make the secret tags and draw a results table.
Run the test blind with 10 pieces of each. Draw the dot plot. Write the report.

projects.record: A one-page report with: the claim, the plan, the table, the dot plot, the claim-evidence-reasoning, how sure you are, and what your test left out.
projects.context: In this project, you test one real claim from start to finish, with ten pieces of each thing, secret tags and a random order. Then you write a report that says how sure you are.

setup.art: A planning board with three columns: what changes, what stays the same, what is measured, written on a large sheet.
setup.caption: 1. Plan the test on a large sheet.

setup.art: Twenty pieces with paper tags marked with letters, and a helper keeping a folded list.
setup.caption: 2. Tag the pieces with secret letters.

setup.art: A dot plot drawn on a large sheet, with the claim, the evidence and the reasoning written beneath.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the dot plot and write the report.

flow.do: Pick one claim you could test. Ask your child to write what changes, what stays the same and what is measured. Ask: how will you make the test fair?
flow.say: What claim are we testing? What changes? What stays the same? What do we measure?
flow.kid: Pick a claim. Write what changes, what stays the same, what you measure.

ask.q: What could make this test unfair?

flow.parent: Good projects are small. Two things, ten pieces each, one measurement. Use the planning board from Claim Detective.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Family Test Report. You choose and plan.

flow.do: 1. Prepare ten pieces of each thing. 2. Ask the helper to tie a secret letter on each piece and keep the list. 3. Draw the order of testing from a bowl. 4. Draw the results table.
flow.say: The helper tags the pieces with secret letters. We test in the order we draw from the bowl. Nobody who tests knows which is which.
flow.kid: Helper: tag the pieces. Tester: draw the order.
flow.parent: The helper can be anyone, even a younger sibling. Keep the list folded until the last number is written.
flow.context: In this step, you prepare the blind test. The tester must not know which is which.

flow.do: Test all twenty pieces in the drawn order. Use the same method each time. Write down every number against its letter.
flow.say: Test each piece the same way. Write the number against its letter. Do not peek at the list.
flow.kid: Test each piece the same way. Write each number.
flow.parent: If a piece is spoiled, write what went wrong and do not hide the number.
flow.context: In this step, you run the test blind. Day 2 begins here.

flow.do: The helper opens the list. Sort the numbers into two groups. Draw a dot plot with two rows. Find the range and the middle value for each.
flow.say: Now open the list. Which letters are which? Draw a dot plot with two rows.
flow.kid: Open the list. Draw two rows of dots.

ask.q: Do the two rows overlap?

flow.context: In this step, you open the list and draw the dot plot.

flow.do: Write the report. Include the claim, the plan, the table and the dot plot. Add claim, evidence and reasoning, how sure you are, and what the test left out. Read it to the family.
flow.say: Write your report. Say what you can honestly claim. Say how sure you are. Say what the test left out. Read it to the family.
flow.kid: Write the report. Read it to the family.
flow.parent: An honest 'we cannot tell' is a good result. A report that says what the test left out is a strong report.

check.q: Your dot plots overlap a lot. What claim can you honestly write?
options: We cannot tell which is better with this test
The one with the bigger middle value is better
The test is wrong
check.why: When the ranges overlap a lot, the wobble is bigger than the difference. The honest claim is that this test cannot tell them apart. A bigger middle value alone is not enough. Saying the test is wrong usually means disliking a result that is not clear.

flow.context: In this step, you write and share the report. This is how real scientists end a test.

challenges.title: Steady Hands: shrink the wobble of a drop
challenges.problem: When you drop a ball by hand ten times, the bounces vary. Build a gadget from cardboard, paper and tape that makes the ten bounces of one ball vary less than they do by hand.
constraints: Use only cardboard, paper, tape and string from home. No electric parts.
The ball must start with its bottom at the same height every time.
You must drop the same ball ten times by hand and ten times with the gadget, in a random order.
Read all bounces from eye level, or with a phone video.
materials: a cardboard tube, such as a paper-towel roll, or a folded sheet of thick paper
masking tape, string and a tape measure
paper and pencil to draw the dot plots
general: A cardboard tube held upright on the floor, with the ball dropped from the top, so it falls straight and lands in the same spot.
A paper funnel taped to a stand, that lets the ball go the same way each time.
A thin card slid out from under the ball to release it, instead of a finger.
creative: A tilted ramp that releases the ball with no spin.
Two tubes, one for the fall and one to catch the ball after the bounce.
A sheet of paper with a hole in it, that holds the ball, and is pulled away.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your gadget. Build it and test it with ten drops. Compare its range with the range of ten hand drops. Change one thing, such as the length of the tube, and test again. Which design gave the smallest range? Why do you think it did?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about cutting down the wobble in a test. You build a dropping gadget and measure how much it narrows the range of the bounces.

flow.do: Read the problem together. First, drop the ball ten times by hand and write the ten heights. Draw the dot plot and find the range.
flow.say: First drop the ball ten times by hand. Write each height. This range is the one to beat.
flow.kid: Drop ten times by hand. Find the range.
flow.parent: Use the same tape measure and floor square as in the Bounce Test.
flow.context: This is the first step of Steady Hands. You find the range to beat.

flow.do: Ask your child to sketch two or three gadgets. Ask what makes the drop vary by hand.
flow.say: Why do the drops vary by hand? What could a gadget do better than fingers?
flow.kid: Sketch two or three gadgets.

ask.q: What causes the wobble when you drop by hand?
good: The fingers let go a little differently.
It lands on a different spot.

flow.context: In this step, you plan. Think about what causes the wobble.

flow.do: Build the first gadget. Drop the ball ten times through it, in a random order mixed with hand drops. Read each bounce. Write the numbers.
flow.say: Build your gadget. Test it ten times. Mix with some hand drops. Draw the order from a bowl.
flow.kid: Build the gadget. Test it ten times.
flow.parent: Mixing hand drops and gadget drops in a random order stops the ball warming up or the tester getting better from favouring one.
flow.context: In this step, you build and test your gadget.

flow.do: Draw both dot plots on one number line. Is the gadget's range smaller? By how much? Change one thing and test again.
flow.say: Compare the ranges. Did the gadget help? Change one thing and test again.
flow.kid: Compare the two ranges. Change one thing and test again.

check.q: The gadget cut the range from 6 centimetres to 2 centimetres. What did the gadget remove?
options: Part of the wobble in how the drop starts
All the wobble in the world
The error in the ruler
check.why: A smaller range means that part of the wobble came from how the ball was released. Some wobble remains, from the floor, the spin and the reading. Choosing 'all the wobble' usually means thinking a better tool makes variation vanish.

flow.context: In this step, you compare and improve.

challenges.title: Pass the Recipe: can another family get your answer?
challenges.problem: Write a recipe for a simple test so clear that another child, who has never seen it, gets close to your answer without asking you anything.
constraints: The test must use only things found in most homes.
The recipe must name every amount, size and time.
Your friend must follow only the written recipe, with no help from you.
Both of you must do at least five tries.
materials: a simple test, such as how far a rubber band stretches with 10 coins
paper and pencil to write the recipe
a friend or a cousin to test it, in person or by phone call
general: Write the recipe as numbered steps, with every size and amount.
Draw the picture for each step, like the step pictures in this unit.
Add a results table to the recipe so the friend writes in the same format.
creative: Film yourself doing the test, and send only the film, not the words.
Write the recipe in two languages, such as English and Tamil or Hindi.
Ask two friends to test it, and compare all three results.
challenges.your_turn: Write the recipe and do the test yourself first. Give it to your friend. Compare the ranges. Where did the recipe leave something out? Fix it, and test again. How close were your answers the second time?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about repeating a test. A good test can be repeated by someone else and give about the same answer. You write a recipe and check whether it works.
