flow.do: Pick a simple test, such as how far a rubber band stretches with 10 coins. Do it five times yourself. Write the five numbers and the range.
flow.say: Do the test five times. Write each number. Find the range. This is your own answer.
flow.kid: Do your test five times. Find the range.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pass the Recipe. You do your own test first.

flow.do: Write the recipe as numbered steps, with every size, amount and time. Add a picture for each step if you can, and a blank results table.
flow.say: Write the recipe. Name every size and every amount. Another child must be able to follow it.
flow.kid: Write the recipe. Name every size and amount.

ask.q: What might your friend not know?

flow.parent: Common gaps: which rubber band, how to hang the coins, whether to measure from the hook or the knot, what to do with the first stretch.
flow.context: In this step, you write the recipe.

flow.do: Give the recipe to your friend. They do the test five times and write their numbers. You do not help.
flow.say: Your friend follows the recipe alone. You do not answer questions. Wait and watch.
flow.kid: Give the recipe to a friend. Do not help.
flow.parent: If the friend is far away, send the recipe by phone and talk afterwards. Resist the urge to explain.
flow.context: In this step, your friend runs the test from your recipe alone.

flow.do: Compare your range with your friend's. Do they overlap? Find one step in the recipe that was unclear. Fix the recipe.
flow.say: Compare your two ranges. Where did the recipe leave something out? Fix it.
flow.kid: Compare your ranges. Fix one unclear step.

check.q: Your answer was 12 to 15 centimetres and your friend's was 12 to 16. What does this tell you?
options: The recipe works well, because the ranges overlap almost fully
The test is wrong
Your friend cheated
check.why: A recipe works when another person gets about the same range. Almost full overlap shows the test can be repeated. Choosing 'the test is wrong' usually means expecting identical numbers, which no test gives.

flow.context: In this step, you compare and fix the recipe.

items.p: You drop the same rubber ball ten times from the same height and get ten slightly different bounces. What is the best explanation?
opts: Many tiny things change a little from drop to drop, such as how your fingers let go and where the ball lands
The ball gets tired and bounces differently each time
The test was done wrongly and the results should be thrown away
items.why: Tiny differences in the release, the landing spot, the spin and the reading add up to a spread. Picking 'done wrongly' usually means expecting a perfect test, and no test is perfect.

items.p: If the same test gives ten different numbers, the tester must have made a mistake.
items.why: False. Variation is normal in every test. The numbers should be close, not equal. Only a number far from the rest needs a second look.

items.p: The gap between the smallest result and the biggest result is called the ____.
items.why: The range tells you how far the results spread. A wide range means the results wobble a lot.

items.p: Put the steps of drawing a dot plot in order.
items: Find the smallest and the biggest result
Draw a number line from the smallest to the biggest
Make one dot above the line for each result
Stack the dots of equal results on top of each other
Look at where dots pile up and where there are gaps
items.a: order shown
items.why: You need to know the smallest and biggest first, so the number line fits. Then each result becomes a dot. Equal results stack. Last, you read the picture.

items.p: Look at the table. Which two balls have ranges that overlap?
opts: The rubber ball and the table-tennis ball
The rubber ball and the marble
The marble and the table-tennis ball
items.why: The rubber ball ranged from 30 to 35 and the table-tennis ball from 31 to 36, so they share the numbers 31 to 35. The marble's 23 to 28 does not touch either of them.
items.context: This question is about the Bounce Test. You drop a rubber ball, a table-tennis ball, a marble and a ball of clay ten times each from 50 centimetres, and look at how much the bounces vary.

chart.title: Made-up bounce heights for 10 drops from 50 centimetres

items.p: Sort each pair of ranges. Do the two ranges overlap, or are they apart?
items.a: see items
items.why: Ranges overlap when they share at least one number. 5 to 9 and 9 to 12 share the 9. 14 to 18 holds all of 15 to 16. 40 to 50 and 51 to 60 miss each other by one.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: Range
The gap from the smallest to the biggest result
Middle value
The result in the middle when all are in order
Zero error
A fault in a tool that is the same size on every reading
Blind test
The tester does not know which sample is which
Control
A sample where you do nothing to the thing you test
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each word names one idea in the unit: how far results spread, the middle of the results, a steady fault in a tool, a test that stops hopes from pushing, and a sample that shows what happens anyway.

items.p: A friend says: 'I dropped a rubber ball once and it bounced to 31 centimetres. I dropped a marble once and it bounced to 25. So the rubber ball is bouncier.' Write two things you would say to your friend.
items.a: One drop of each is only one drop. Drop each ten times and draw a dot plot. If the two ranges do not touch, you can say there is a real difference. If the ranges overlap, you cannot tell.
items.why: One drop shows no spread. Many drops show the spread, and the ranges decide whether the difference is real.

items.p: Ten bounces in order are 30, 30, 31, 31, 32, 32, 33, 33, 34, 35. What is the middle value?
items.why: With ten results, the middle is between the fifth and sixth. Both are 32, so the middle value is 32. Picking 35 means picking the biggest, and 31 means counting from the wrong end.

items.p: If one ball has a bigger middle value than another ball, it is always the better ball.
items.why: False. If the ranges overlap a lot, another set of drops could reverse the order. A difference is real only when it is bigger than the wobble.

items.p: A ruler's first centimetre has broken off, so it starts at the 1 centimetre mark. A strip really measures 10 centimetres. What does this ruler read when the strip's end lines up with the end of the ruler?
items.why: The ruler starts counting at 1, so every reading is 1 too big. This is a zero error. Picking 9 usually means thinking a missing piece makes a ruler read less.

items.p: A test in which the tester does not know which sample is which is called a ____ test.
items.why: A blind test stops the tester's hopes from nudging the result without them knowing.

items.p: Draw a dot plot for these five bounce heights, in centimetres: 30, 32, 32, 33, 35.
items.a: A number line from 30 to 35. One dot above 30, two dots stacked above 32, one dot above 33 and one dot above 35. The range is 5 centimetres.
items.why: Each result becomes a dot on the number line. Equal results stack. The range is the gap between the smallest and the biggest dot.
items.art: A number line from 30 to 35 with five dots above it, two of them stacked at 32.

items.p: Why do scientists draw the order of testing from a bowl?
opts: So that no sample always goes first or last
So that the tester can guess the result
So that the samples get tired
items.why: A random order gives every sample a fair chance of an early slot and a late slot. Choosing 'takes longer' misses the reason: order can quietly change results.

items.p: Does each fault push every reading the same way, or make readings wobble?
items: A ruler with a chipped end
A thermometer that reads 2 degrees too high
Reading a fast bounce by eye
A cloth tape that has stretched
A ball landing on slightly different spots
items.a: see items
items.why: A zero error or a stretched tape adds the same push to each reading. Hidden nicks, fast bounces and different landing spots make the numbers wobble from try to try.

items.p: Jothi wants to find out if a new kind of kitchen paper is stronger than the old kind. She has time to test only 20 strips. Her family has different plans.

views.says: Test 10 strips of each kind, in a random order, and draw a dot plot.
Test all 20 strips of the new kind, because the new kind is the one we care about.
Test just 3 strips of each. That is enough for a rough idea.

items.ask: Whose plan would you choose? Give one reason. Then say what one other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer chooses Jothi's plan. Ten strips of each kind lets her compare two ranges. Testing only the new paper gives no comparison. Three each gives a very rough picture. The aunt has a point that a small test gives a rough idea quickly, and the father is right that the new paper is the one to know about.
items.why: The question is a fair comparison. A comparison needs both kinds, a fair number of tries and a random order.

items.p: Five strips held 14, 22, 17, 19 and 9 coins. What is the middle value?
items.why: In order the strips are 9, 14, 17, 19 and 22. The middle one is 17. Picking 16.2 gives the average, which is 81 divided by 5. The average is pulled down by the 9.

items.p: The average and the middle value are always the same number.
items.why: False. For 9, 14, 17, 19 and 22, the average is 16.2 and the middle value is 17. A very low or high result pulls the average but not the middle value.

items.p: Two labs test the same rope. Lab A says it holds 200 kilograms and Lab B says 150 kilograms. What is the best next step?
opts: Check whether they used the same method, the same sample size and the same speed, then repeat with one agreed method
items.why: Different methods give different numbers. A standard test fixes the method, so labs can agree. Believing one lab without checking is a bet.

items.p: Does each action help a fair test or hurt it?
items: Drawing the order from a bowl
Testing the new bag three times and the old bag once
A helper hiding the names with codes
Writing down only the results that agree with your guess
Reading every bounce from eye level
Telling the tasters which one is Premium
items.a: see items
items.why: A random order, secret codes and the same way of reading help. Giving one sample more tries, hiding results and telling tasters the label push the result.

items.p: An advert says: 'This bag is 30 per cent stronger.' Write three questions you would ask before believing it.
items.a: Stronger than what? How many bags were tested, and how many tries? How much did the results wobble, and did the ranges overlap? Who did the test?
items.why: A number without a comparison, a number of tries and the spread cannot be checked.

items.p: Arrows land close together, but far from the middle of the target. Which two words fit?
items.why: Close together means the readings agree, which is precise. Far from the middle means they are not near the true size, which is not accurate. A tool with a zero error gives this pattern.

items.p: Match each problem to a fix.
pairs: A bounce that is too fast for the eye
Film it and look frame by frame
A ruler with a zero error
Check it against another ruler
A tester who knows which sample is which
Use secret codes and a helper
Always testing one cloth first
Draw the order from a bowl
Only two tries
Do ten tries and draw a dot plot
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each fault has a fix. Slow motion helps the eyes, a second ruler finds a zero error, codes stop hopes, a random order stops order effects, and more tries show the spread.

items.p: Put the steps of a blind test in order.
items: A helper puts secret codes on the samples and keeps the list
Draw the order of testing from a bowl
Test every sample the same way and write each result against its code
Write down every result, including odd ones
Open the list and sort the results by sample
items.a: order shown
items.why: The helper prepares first. Then the order is drawn. The tester tests without knowing. All numbers are written. Only at the end does the list open.

items.p: Draw two targets. On the first, show arrows that are precise but not accurate. On the second, show arrows that are accurate on average but not precise. Label each one.
items.a: First target: all arrows in a tight group off to one side. Second target: arrows spread widely, but scattered evenly around the middle.
items.why: Precise means readings agree with each other. Accurate means they are close to the true size.
items.art: Two round targets side by side, one with a tight cluster of arrows near the edge and one with arrows spread around the centre.

items.p: Clever Hans, the horse, answered correctly even when the person asking did not know the answer.
items.why: False. When the questioner did not know the answer, or Hans could not see the questioner, he got it wrong. He was following tiny movements that people made without knowing.

items.p: A wear test rubs a cloth on sandpaper until a hole appears. What does it leave out about real life?
items.why: The test copies rubbing, but a real cloth also faces sunlight, washing and sweat. A test answers only the question it asks.

items.p: A sample where you do nothing to the thing you test, so that you can see what happens anyway, is called a ____.
items.why: A control shows what changes by itself, so you do not give a cause the credit for something else.

items.p: In the Secret Code Test, all four cloth squares were cut from one cloth. Explain why people could still give different scores.
items.a: The label can push a person's score up or down without them knowing, which is bias. Also, touch is rough. A person's score can wobble from one moment to the next, even for the same square. The blind round shows how much is just wobble.
items.why: Scores include a push from the label and a wobble from the person. The blind round takes away the push.

items.p: A school ruler has a worn end, so it reads 1 centimetre too big. Three children disagree about what to do.

views.says: Throw it away. A faulty tool cannot give true results.
Keep it. Subtract 1 from every reading, or check it against another ruler first.
Keep it for measuring differences, because the error cancels out. Do not use it for sizes.

items.ask: Who is right? Give one reason. Say what another person has right.
items.a: Imran and the teacher use the fault wisely. A steady fault can be found and removed. In a difference between two readings, the same error cancels. Anjali is right that it is not safe for measuring a true size without a correction.
items.why: A zero error is the same on every reading, so it can be found and handled. A wobbling error cannot.

items.p: A dot plot shows 3 dots at 31, 2 dots at 33 and 1 dot at 40. The range is ____ centimetres.
items.why: The range is the biggest minus the smallest. 40 minus 31 is 9. The dot at 40 is odd and widens the range a lot, which is a reason to check that drop.

items.p: A lift cable is tested on many pieces. The middle piece broke at 20 tonnes and the weakest broke at 14 tonnes. The lift will carry 2 tonnes. Which number does an engineer worry about most?
opts: 14, because the weakest piece sets how safe the cable is
20, because the middle is the usual
items.why: A cable can contain a weak piece. Safety comes from the weakest, with a big gap between it and the load. Choosing 20 usually means trusting the middle too much.

items.p: Which is the best claim from a dot plot where two ranges overlap a lot?
opts: We cannot tell which is better with this test
The bigger middle value is better
items.why: When ranges overlap a lot, the wobble is bigger than the gap. The honest claim says the test cannot tell. Saying 'exactly the same' goes too far, because a bigger test might show a small difference.

items.p: In the Eight Matchboxes game, 4 of 8 boxes are heavy. A player picks 4 boxes at random. There are 70 ways to pick 4 boxes from 8. In how many of these 70 ways are all 4 chosen boxes heavy?
items.why: Only one choice of four is exactly the four heavy boxes. So the chance of finding all four by luck is 1 in 70.
items.context: This question is about the Eight Matchboxes activity. A helper fills four boxes with more coins and four with fewer, mixes them up, and you try to pick out the heavy ones by feel.

items.p: So the chance of finding all four heavy boxes by luck alone is 1 in ____.
items.why: One lucky way out of 70 possible ways gives all four heavy boxes. That is why finding all four several times in a row would be strong evidence of skill.

items.p: In one round you find 3 of the 4 heavy boxes. Explain why this one round is not strong evidence that your hands are good.
items.a: There are 16 ways to find exactly 3, and 1 way to find all 4. So 17 of the 70 ways give 3 or more right. That is about 1 time in 4. It happens fairly often by luck. More rounds are needed.
items.why: A result that luck gives about one time in four is not strong evidence. Repeating the test gives stronger evidence.
items.context: This question is about the Eight Matchboxes activity, where you sort boxes by feel and a helper counts how many heavy boxes you found.

items.p: A chemist makes a cloudy, thin liquid that is not what she expected. Her colleagues argue about it.

views.says: Pour it away. It does not fit the plan, so it is a failed test.
Keep it and test it, but write down what it is and how it was made.
Test it three times only. If the results are odd again, forget it.

items.ask: Whose advice would you follow? Give one reason. Say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer chooses to keep and test it. Odd results can be slips or discoveries, and testing finds out which. Colleague 3 is right that a few repeats are a sensible start, and Colleague 1 is right that many odd results are mistakes. Throwing it away risks losing a discovery.
items.why: An odd result needs to be checked. Deleting it hides evidence. Repeating it, and writing down its cause, is what finds the truth.

items.p: A cloth test gives 20 for cloth A and 22 for cloth B, with ranges that overlap a lot. A buyer must choose one. What else should she think about?
opts: Price, how the cloth will be used and the weakest piece in each
Nothing, because the test says they are equal
items.why: When a test cannot tell two things apart, other facts decide: cost, use and the weak end of the range. Choosing 'the bigger number' ignores the wobble.

items.p: Does each test break the thing, or leave it whole?
items: Pulling a paper strip until it tears
Tapping a pot and listening to the ring
Bending a paper clip until it snaps
Shining ultrasound into a railway line
Looking at a bridge through a magnifier for cracks
Loading a rope until it snaps
items.a: see items
items.why: Some tests ask 'how much can it take?' and must break the sample. Others look for hidden cracks without harm. Engineers use both.

items.p: A test can prove that a rope will never break.
items.why: False. A test can show how a rope behaved on the day, but not what will happen on every day to come. Engineers talk about how likely a failure is, and keep inspecting.

items.p: Match each fault to an example.
pairs: Bias
A tester pulls the cloth she hopes will lose a bit faster
Order effect
The last cloth is tested when the tester's arms are tired
Zero error
A ruler with a chipped end
Variation
Ten strips from one roll hold different loads
Control
A strip left dry beside the strips that are wetted
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each example shows a different thing: a hope that pushes, an order that favours, a steady fault in a tool, a natural spread in the material, and a sample that does nothing.

items.p: A ball dropped from 50 centimetres bounces to 30 centimetres. What fraction of the drop height did it keep?
items.why: The ball kept 30 of the 50 centimetres. 30 divided by 50 is 0.6, which is the same as 3 out of 5. The rest of the energy went into sound and warmth.

items.p: Draw a plan for a blind test of two kinds of tissue paper. Show who does what, and how the order is chosen.
items.a: A helper tags 10 pieces of each kind with secret letters and keeps the list. The tester draws chits to set the order, tests each piece the same way, and writes the number against its letter. At the end the helper opens the list and the numbers are sorted into two dot plots.
items.why: A blind test needs a helper with a secret list, a random order, one method for all pieces and a list opened only at the end.
items.art: A diagram with three people: a helper with a folded list, a tester with a bowl of chits, and a table of tagged tissue pieces.

items.p: If two labs get different numbers for the same rope, at least one lab is cheating.
items.why: False. Different methods, speeds, air or samples can give honestly different numbers. This is why labs agree on standard tests and compare.

items.p: Seeds from one packet sprout on different days in the same pot. Say how this spread could help the seeds when the monsoon is late in some years.
items.a: If all seeds sprouted on the same day and the rains were late, they might all die. Seeds that sprout on different days give a chance that some meet the rain. The spread works like a safety margin for the plant.
items.why: Variation in a group, such as sprouting day, can protect the group when the future is not certain.

items.p: Why do labs in different countries agree on standard tests?
opts: So that results from different places can be compared
So that every lab gets the same answer by magic
So that no one needs to repeat a test
items.why: A standard fixes the size of the sample, the speed and the air, so results from different labs can be compared. It does not remove the wobble, but it makes comparisons fair.

items.p: A test that rubs a material again and again to find how long it lasts is called a ____ test.
items.why: A wear test copies rubbing in real use, in a shorter time.

items.p: A weaver in Kanchipuram says she can feel with her fingers whether a silk thread is strong. A factory wants to pull every thread on a machine. They disagree.

views.says: My fingers have felt thousands of threads. I know a weak one when I feel it.
Pull every thread on a machine. A number is the same for everyone.
Use a blind test to check the weaver's hands against the machine, then decide how to use both.

items.ask: Whose plan would you choose? Give one reason. Say what another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer values both. The weaver's hands carry long experience and are quick, but they need checking. The machine gives numbers but can miss what hands feel. A blind test, as the teacher says, finds out how good the hands are, and the two together can be better than either one.
items.why: Experience and measurement can check each other. A blind test gives a fair way to compare.

quiz.p: What does repeating a test ten times show you that one try cannot?
opts: The exact true size of the thing
That the first try was wrong
quiz.why: Ten tries show the spread, so you know how much to trust one number. Picking 'the exact true size' is common but wrong: repeating shows the wobble, not the perfect number.

quiz.p: Two groups of results have ranges 40 to 55 and 52 to 70. What can you honestly say?
opts: We cannot tell if they are really different, because the ranges overlap
quiz.why: The ranges share the numbers 52 to 55, so the wobble is bigger than the gap. Choosing 'certainly bigger' ignores the overlap.

quiz.p: Six results in order are 12, 13, 14, 16, 17, 19. What are the range and the middle value?
quiz.why: The range is 19 minus 12, which is 7. With six results, the middle is between 14 and 16, so the middle value is 15. Picking 14 means taking only the third result.

quiz.p: A ruler with a chipped end reads 1 centimetre too much on every strip. What kind of fault is this?
opts: A zero error, which is the same on every reading
A random wobble that changes each time
quiz.why: The error is steady and comes from the tool. It can be found by comparing with another ruler. Choosing 'random wobble' mixes up two kinds of fault.

quiz.p: Why is a helper who knows the secret list not the tester?
opts: The tester must not know which sample is which, so hopes cannot nudge the result
The helper is better at measuring
quiz.why: A blind test works because the tester cannot favour any sample. Choosing 'faster' misses the reason.

quiz.p: Why is a random order better than 'start with my favourite'?
opts: Because no sample always goes first or last
Because the tester can finish early
Because favourites are always the strongest
quiz.why: An order can quietly change results as the tester tires or the materials change. A random order gives every sample the same chances.

quiz.p: A bag for the monsoon is tested only when dry. What is the main problem?
opts: The test does not copy the real job, so it may not be valid
The test uses too many tries
quiz.why: A test is valid if it measures what you care about. A bag meets rain, so its wet strength matters. A dry test answers a different question.

quiz.p: Which claim best says how sure you are?
opts: The rubber ball bounces higher. I am fairly sure, because the ranges do not touch, but I tested on only one floor.
The rubber ball is the best ball.
quiz.why: A good claim names the evidence, the reasoning and its limits. The other sentences give no evidence or go too far.

quiz.p: Repeating a test a hundred times will fix a ruler with a zero error.
quiz.why: False. Repeating shrinks the effect of luck but not a fault that pushes every reading the same way.

quiz.p: In a test of tissue strength, one strip is left dry in the same room while the others are wetted. What is the dry strip?
quiz.why: A control gets everything except the thing being tested. It shows what changes anyway.

open_questions.q: Is anything in nature exactly repeatable, or is some wobble built into the world?
open_questions.why_open: At the smallest scale, physicists still argue whether chance is built into nature or only hides a pattern we cannot see.

open_questions.q: How many tries are enough to be sure about a material that must never fail?
open_questions.why_open: Engineers use maths to estimate, but the answer depends on how rare the failure is. For very rare failures, no test can be large enough.

open_questions.q: Can a computer predict how a given piece of material will break before it is tested?
open_questions.why_open: Computers can predict the usual, but the exact first crack in one piece depends on tiny flaws that no one can see.

open_questions.q: How much do our hopes change our results without us knowing?
open_questions.why_open: Psychologists keep finding new ways in which expectation changes what we see. Nobody has a full list.

open_questions.q: Why do living things keep so much variation, even when it seems wasteful?
open_questions.why_open: Biologists agree that variation helps groups survive changes, but they still argue about how much variation is the right amount.

open_questions.q: Will a perfect test of 'strong' ever be found, one that works for every job?
open_questions.why_open: Strong means different things for pulling, bending, hitting and wearing, so there may be no single best test.

maths.problem: The ten bounce heights of the rubber ball are 31, 33, 30, 34, 32, 31, 35, 30, 33 and 32 centimetres. Add them and divide by 10. What is the average? How does it compare with the middle value, which is 32?
maths.answer: The average is 32.1 centimetres. It is very close to the middle value of 32.
maths.explain: The ten heights add up to 321. Dividing by 10 gives 32.1. The middle value is 32. They are close because there is no odd result pulling the average. If one drop had been 50, the average would jump and the middle value would hardly move.
maths.context: In the Bounce Test, you drop each ball ten times and write every bounce height.
maths.why_maths: The average and the middle value are two ways to sum up a pile of results. Comparing them tells you whether an odd result is pulling the picture.

maths.problem: In the Bounce Test, the rubber ball's middle value was 32 and the marble's was 25. Each ball's ten drops had a range of 5. Is the gap between the middle values bigger or smaller than the range? What does this tell you?
maths.answer: The gap is 7, which is bigger than the range of 5. The difference is real.
maths.explain: 32 take away 25 is 7. The gap of 7 is bigger than the wobble of 5 in each ball. So the marble's drops are not just a lucky low set. A difference bigger than the wobble can be believed.
maths.context: In the Bounce Test, you compare the middle values and the ranges of different balls.
maths.why_maths: Comparing a gap with a spread is the quickest check on whether a difference is real.

maths.problem: A ball is dropped from 50 centimetres and bounces to 32 centimetres. What fraction of its drop height did it keep? Write it as a decimal and as a percentage.
maths.answer: 32 out of 50, which is 0.64 or 64 per cent.
maths.explain: 32 over 50 is the same as 64 over 100, because both numbers can be doubled. 64 over 100 is 0.64, or 64 per cent. The ball kept about two thirds of its height. The rest left as sound and warmth.
maths.context: In the Bounce Test, you drop each ball from 50 centimetres and measure how high it bounces.
maths.why_maths: A fraction of the drop height lets you compare balls dropped from different heights, and says how much energy the ball gives back.

maths.problem: If each bounce keeps about 64 per cent of the last height, and the first bounce was 32 centimetres, about how high is the second bounce? Round to the nearest centimetre.
maths.explain: 64 per cent of 32 is 32 times 0.64. 32 times 0.6 is 19.2. 32 times 0.04 is 1.28. Together they are 20.48. To the nearest centimetre, that is 20. A real second bounce may be a little different, because every bounce wobbles.
maths.context: In the Bounce Test, each ball bounces lower each time. Here you predict the next bounce.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying by the fraction kept lets you predict the next bounce before you drop the ball, and then check the prediction.

maths.problem: In the Eight Matchboxes activity, there are 70 ways to pick 4 boxes from 8. One way finds all four heavy boxes. Sixteen ways find exactly 3 heavy boxes. What fraction of the 70 ways gives 3 or more heavy boxes? About how often is that?
maths.answer: 17 out of 70, which is about 1 time in 4.
maths.explain: 1 plus 16 is 17. So 17 of the 70 ways give 3 or more. 70 divided by 17 is a little over 4. So about 1 time in 4 you would find 3 or more by pure luck. This is why one good round is not enough evidence.
maths.context: In the Eight Matchboxes activity, you sort heavy boxes from light boxes by feel and compare your score with pure luck.
maths.why_maths: Counting the ways luck can give a good score shows how strong your evidence is.

maths.problem: In the Rub Test, the middle values of rubs until a hole were: thin cotton 45, polyester 70, kitchen duster 62 and old jeans 100 or more. A cloth is rubbed 40 times a minute. How many minutes does the polyester need to reach its middle value? And how many minutes of rubbing does thin cotton need?
maths.answer: Polyester: 70 divided by 40 is 1 and three-quarter minutes, which is about 1 minute 45 seconds. Thin cotton: 45 divided by 40 is a little over 1 minute.
maths.explain: 70 divided by 40 is 1.75 minutes, which is 1 minute and 45 seconds. 45 divided by 40 is 1.125 minutes, which is about 1 minute 8 seconds. So the whole wear test for cotton takes about a minute, but copies much longer of real use.
maths.context: In the Rub Test, you slide a cloth-covered katori along sandpaper and count rubs until a hole shows.
maths.why_maths: Turning rubs into minutes shows how an accelerated test squeezes a long time of use into a short test.

maths.problem: A katori goes 20 centimetres along the sandpaper and 20 centimetres back for each rub. How far, in metres, does the cloth travel in 60 rubs?
maths.explain: One rub is 20 plus 20, which is 40 centimetres. 60 rubs are 60 times 40, which is 2,400 centimetres. 100 centimetres make 1 metre, so 2,400 centimetres is 24 metres. The cloth is rubbed over a long distance in a small space.
maths.context: In the Rub Test, each rub is a trip of 20 centimetres each way along the sandpaper.
maths.why_maths: Changing centimetres to metres lets you picture how much rubbing the cloth has had.

maths.problem: A school bag is carried twice a day on 200 school days. Say one carry does as much damage to a strap as 10 rubs on the machine, which does 40 rubs a minute. How many minutes does the machine need to copy one school year?
maths.explain: 2 carries a day on 200 days is 400 carries. 400 carries times 10 rubs is 4,000 rubs. 4,000 divided by 40 rubs a minute is 100 minutes. So a year of carrying is copied in about an hour and forty minutes. The number 10 rubs per carry is a guess, so the answer is a rough one.
maths.context: In the Rub Test, you copy the wear of real use with a machine that rubs the cloth quickly.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying and dividing shows how a machine can squeeze a year of use into one afternoon. The guess in the middle also shows how much a test depends on its assumptions.

maths.problem: A paper bag costs 6 rupees and holds a middle value of 40 coins. A jute bag costs 30 rupees and holds 50 coins. How many rupees does each bag cost for every coin it holds? Which is cheaper for each coin?
maths.answer: Paper: 6 divided by 40 is 0.15 rupees, or 15 paise. Jute: 30 divided by 50 is 0.60 rupees, or 60 paise. The paper bag is cheaper for each coin.
maths.explain: 6 divided by 40 is 0.15. 30 divided by 50 is 0.6. The paper bag costs 15 paise for each coin, and the jute bag 60 paise. But a jute bag can be used many times, so the best choice also depends on how long each bag lasts.
maths.context: This question is about the choice between two bags after a strength test, where one holds 40 coins and the other 50 coins.
maths.why_maths: A test number becomes more useful when you divide it by cost. It shows that the best material depends on more than one number.

maths.problem: A lift cable is made so that its middle piece breaks at 20 tonnes and its weakest piece at 14 tonnes. The lift carries at most 2 tonnes. How many times bigger than the load is the weakest piece, and how many times bigger is the middle piece?
maths.answer: The weakest piece is 7 times the load. The middle piece is 10 times the load.
maths.explain: 14 divided by 2 is 7. 20 divided by 2 is 10. A safety factor of 7 is the smaller of the two, and it is the one engineers trust. The gap between 7 and 10 shows why the spread matters.
maths.context: This question is about a lift cable, where tests on many pieces show a weakest piece and a middle piece.
maths.why_maths: Dividing by the load shows how many times stronger than needed a cable is, and why the weakest piece must be used.

roots.context: We have dropped balls, drawn dots, and learned that no test gives the same number twice. Now we ask what that means for the things around us, and for ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Drop one ball ten times and you get ten different heights. Often the wobble in one ball is wider than the gap between two balls. So a ball has no single bounce. It has a habit, a range of bounces.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'this ball bounces 31 centimetres' or 'this paper holds 14 coins' as if one number belonged to the thing, like its colour. That leaves out the wobble every test shows.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Bounce Test, each ball's ten drops spread over several centimetres, and some balls' ranges overlapped. In made-up results, the rubber ball and the table-tennis ball overlapped almost completely. Your own dots will show how wide your wobble is. Write them as they are.

three.who_am_i: You never run to the gate in exactly the same time twice. What you can do is a range, and so is what you are like, from day to day.
three.what_is_life: Seeds from one packet sprout on different days, in the same pot. This variation is how a group of living beings can meet a late monsoon, a new disease or a hot summer.
three.what_is_this_world: Even a ball, with no choice at all, will not do the same thing twice. Many tiny causes, such as a speck of dust or a slightly different touch, add up. The world repeats its patterns, but never exactly.

roots.thread: Every test in this unit gave a spread. The same ball, the same strip and the same grain of rice each gave a range of numbers. A material does not have one bounce, one strength or one length. It has a habit that shows up as a range. We learned to describe that range with dots, a range and a middle value. And we learned that our own hopes and tools add their own wobble. A believable result states the habit, the wobble and how sure we are. Saying 'it is exactly this' is a small untruth, even when it is a handy one.

science.text: Every measurement has some spread. The spread within a group is measured and reported in every science, from chemistry to medicine.
Whether the smallest events in nature are truly random, or hide a pattern we cannot yet see, is argued by physicists.
Variation inside a group of living beings is the raw material of evolution, as Charles Darwin described in 1859.

other_view.view: A thing does have one true size, like a ball's real bounciness. The spread is only the error in our tests. With a perfect test, every drop would give the same number. They would say the wobble is a fault in our tools and hands, not part of the ball. So we should try to shrink the wobble, and not call it part of the thing.

practice.title: Ten claps, none the same
practice.say: Sit comfortably. Clap your hands once, and listen. Now clap nine more times, trying to make each clap exactly the same. Listen to each one. No two are quite alike. playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if in a city flat today, but not yet tried with a child. Bounce Test: a tailor's tape taped up a wall gives a long enough scale. Soft floors such as carpet or a mat give very low bounces, so a tile, a board or a thick book goes under the taped square. Forty drops with two readers take about 45 minutes. Reading a fast bounce by eye is hard, and a gap of 1 to 3 centimetres between two readers is normal and is part of the lesson. The clay or foil ball will give 0 every time. If a family has only one ball that bounces, the marble and the clay ball still show a real difference. Secret Code Test: needs at least 5 people, so a neighbour or a video call may be needed. The label effect is not guaranteed in a small group, and the unit says so. All four squares are cut from one cloth, and everyone is told the truth afterwards. Rub Test: the loading is a starting guess. A katori with about 30 one-rupee coins and coarse sandpaper usually wears a thin cotton through in under 100 rubs, but denim may not wear through at all, and the steps say what to do then. Sandpaper dust is a safety note, and each run uses a fresh lane so lint does not change the next run. Eight Matchboxes: a difference of 2 coins is a fair start, with advice to make it easier or harder. Wet or Dry: the wet strips often tear at the peg, and the step says to try a new strip. The spine is the Bounce Test with the explanations, Roots and quiz, in about two sessions of 45 to 50 minutes. Facts to check before release: the Clever Hans dates and details, the Stephanie Kwolek account of 1965, the Dan Shechtman dates, and the Tirukkural couplet number. The story numbers and the rope company are made up.
